maintopic: CHANGE OF AFFILIATION OF MEMBER FOR RICHELIEU
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, never in all my life have I ever faced a more crucial decision, as a member of Parliament and as a Quebecer. For Quebecers the time has come to choose, and when all is said and done, I must choose Quebec.
Our ambiguous position as a people is not new. Since the earliest years of cohabitation with the anglophone component of this country, we have been treated as a conquered people but, nevertheless, citizens of this great country.
In 1763, James Murray, the first British governor said, in referring to our ancestors, that if they had left it would have been a great loss for the British empire. But what has been done since then to urge us to become full-fledged members of this empire?
Since the Royal Proclamation of 1763, the avowed goal of our new conquerors was to assimilate us. However, out of fear for the Americans and to soothe our feelings, we were recognized as a distinct society, several years later, in the Quebec Act. When at the end of the eighteenth century, repeated demands for our own legislative assembly were finally met, it was without the powers normally bestowed on that body. How magnanimous! How democratic!
We built this country with our blood and sweat. Our thanks was to be humiliated and treated as a people without history and without a culture. As the founding people of this country, we shall never forget the many times we have been humiliated in this great country we
thought was ours: the Conquest, Louis Papineau and the patriots, the Act of Union, Louis Riel, the conscription question in both wars, the War Measures Act, the 1982 patriation of the Constitution without Quebec, and the defeat of the Meech Lake Accord.
History seems to be repeating itself today. I am thinking of that memorable motion presented before the Quebec Legislative Assembly in 1917 by MLA Fran-coeur. He pointed out that the province of Quebec would be willing to accept the break-up of the federative pact of 1867, if the other provinces felt that Quebec was a barrier to Canada's unity, progress and development.
I never thought I would see the day that we would be considered a barrier to Canada's progress and development, despite the "night of the long knives", in 1982. I really believed the risk was worth taking, and that is what made me go into politics in 1984, like most of my colleagues in the Quebec caucus who wanted to defend the interests of Quebec. I was prepared to follow this through to the very end, and I did.
Mr. Speaker, I also believed that the Premiers of the other Canadian provinces would abide by the Meech Lake Accord. I believed that all these politicians were men of their word and would abide by what they had signed. I believed they would never let themselves be manipulated behind the scenes by the Chretien-Trudeau clan. You do not build a country on weakness, and Quebecers will no longer be satisfied with a vision of Canada that, as far as I am concerned, goes back to the Dark Ages.
For weeks I have been literally tom between my loyalty to the Prime Minister and my desire to respond to the imperative interests of Quebec. However, Mr. Speaker, the fact that Quebec was unable to re-enter Canadian Confederation with honour and enthusiasm is certainly not Prime Minister Mulroney's fault. If there ever was a prime minister in the history of Quebec, since 1867, who has done everything to try to give Quebec its proper place in Confederation, he is certainly the one, and I want to take this opportunity to thank him for

June 26, 1990
House of Commons
doing so. We cannot reverse the course of events, however.
Mr. Speaker, I have far too much respect for my compatriots to give them a false impression of the way things stand today. No more expressions of trust in Canada! No more compromises that would be even more humiliating! My pride and dignity need time to heal, and from now on, I want to devote my energies only to Quebec. Quebecers are experiencing a time of extraordinary solidarity, and I would have lifelong regrets if I were to miss out on this new rendezvous with history.
From now on, Mr. Speaker, I intend to sit in this House as an independent, in a Quebec bloc where I will continue to serve the interests of my constituents in the riding of Richelieu, while at the same time serving those of Quebec. I will never forget the trust and encouragement I received from the people of Richelieu during the past weeks. I want to thank them and can assure them that I will continue to devote the same energy to all issues in my riding.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Prime Minister and my Quebec colleagues for the great satisfaction I had in working with them. All good things must come to an end, however and now the curtain rises on the federal tragi-comical farce. Mr. Speaker, a good memory is essential if reason is to prevail. I remember, and I want our descendants to remember. I will never accept the legacy of Lord Durham. And above all, I want Quebecers to look to the future with pride, dignity, determination and without any constraints on their aspirations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that today we must draw conclusions from the events of recent weeks in Canada.
Obviously, the utmost was done to make the whole country accept what all Quebecers always considered to be a bare minimum. I want to say that I am not criticizing Mr. Mulroney; he has full marks from me for his tenacity
and his efforts to bring Quebec into the Constitution with honour, although the enthusiasm disappeared several weeks ago.
It is very clear that Mr. Bourassa went as far as he could possibly go in being open to the efforts made. We must admit that we have all failed. We were unable to repair the constitutional mess that Pierre Elliott Trudeau and Jean Chretien left us. We must begin again, on a different basis, the thorough reform of this country's political institutions if we want them to correspond to the ideas of the distinct societies that make them up.
Most Quebecers who joined or supported the Progressive Conservative Party did so as part of what Rene Levesque called the beau risque, or risk worth taking. I think that we were right and I trust that all our efforts were not completely in vain. Several provincial premiers seem to understand Quebec's aspirations better, and that is a gain. They will really need this understanding in the coming months to explain the consequences of the failure of the Meech Lake Accord to their fellow citizens! Quebecers have now begun to take a different approach, with realism, dignity and determination.
Like them, I am now convinced that beyond party politics, we will give ourselves a country in our image. I am convinced that it will be open to the world, ready to co-operate with its neighbours and all who want to leave their children a country they can identify with.
At a time of globalization of trade, such a move may seem inappropriate at first glance, but how much energy and time have been wasted repairing a constitution that divides us! Perhaps a broad political and social consensus is as necessary for economic development as an abundance of capital and technology. To meet the challenges facing us, we must soon acquire political institutions that express and harness our collective will.
With this deep conviction that is widely shared by my constituents in Rosemont, I have decided to fully support the non-partisan movement launched by the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Bouchard).
I therefore announce my resignation as parliamentary secretary and my decision to sit henceforth as an independent member.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Cadieux (for the Minister of the Environment) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-78, an act to establish a federal environmental assessment process, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of the Environment, who is attending the vitally important London conference on the ozone layer, a conference at which I hope that he and other ministers from around the world will have a great deal of success in terms of strengthening the protocol, it gives me a great deal of satisfaction to begin second reading debate
Government Orders
on one of the most important pieces of legislation to be placed before this House in many years.
The Canadian Environment Assessment Act will be the cornerstone of this government's commitment to environmentally sensible decision making. This bill will change the decisions we make in the future by changing the way we make decisions. It will enable this government to give real effect to the concept of environmentally sustainable economic development.
We will ensure, by implementing the requirements of this bill, that the environment and the economy become unified as an integral concept that will allow us to leave for our grandchildren an environment capable of satisfying their needs.
During the last two decades, Canadians have become increasingly aware of the importance of maintaining both a strong economy and a healthy natural environment. To help satisfy these goals, Canadian governments, both federal and provincial, established environmental assessment processes. Environmental assessment is a systematic method of identifying potential environmental consequences and their impact on people. By identifying adverse environment effects before they occur, plans can be altered so that unwanted environmental impacts are minimized or, ideally, eliminated. In some cases proposals must be abandoned if negative impacts are unacceptable and cannot be mitigated.
Environmental assessment as a planning tool has been practised by the Government of Canada since 1974. It has been used to predict the potential environmental effects of proposals requiring a federal government decision. The process was updated in 1977 and reinforced in 1984 when the environmental assessment and review process guidelines were issued by Order in Council.
These processes were never adequately implemented because a series of governments failed to provide a substantive legislative footing for them. The process was never more than a cabinet directive until 1984, not

June 26, 1990
Government Orders
adequately resourced by government and not sincerely implemented by departments. After 1984 it was still very difficult, even for a government dedicated to environmental values to implement fully the poorly conceived and ambiguously worded guideline order, frantically introduced at that time in a futile attempt to bolster the sagging fortunes of the government of the moment.
In 1987 the government asked the Minister of the Environment to consult the public on the need for and manner of reforming the environmental assessment and review process. The minister issued a Green Paper to serve as a basis for that consultation.
Six months of public meetings were held in major centres across Canada, followed by a national consultative workshop in March, 1988. Broad consultations were held with a wide spectrum of Canadians including governments, the private sector, native peoples, environmental and other special interest groups, the legal profession, and environmental assessment professionals.
Participants in the consultations called for an accountable and administratively simple process based in law that is effective, efficient, fair, and open.
This government has responded clearly and strongly to the needs of the country and of the Canadian people. As a reflection of the consultative process and its promise during the last election campaign and subsequent Speech from the Throne, we are proud to introduce a substantive, important package of reforms to Canada's environmental assessment system which will, as the Minister of the Environment stated last week in launching the initiative, make this the most comprehensive and effective environmental assessment process in the world.
The key element in these reforms is the bill we are discussing today-the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act; for the first time, a comprehensive, legislative commitment to good decision making. While the focus of our debate will be on the legislation this House is being asked to consider, I wish to point out to members of this House that the government is going even further to ensure that this package fills the needs of today's Canadians. We are not stopping with the introduction of Bill C-78.
Beginning immediately we are requiring that environmental factors be integrated into all government policy
decisions. This is an unprecedented step. I cannot overstate its importance to government decision making. Government policies are often the determining factor regarding what economic development projects are conceived and implemented across Canada. If the policies are not environmentally sensitive, it is much more difficult to ensure that the resulting projects will be, even with tough assessment legislation such as we are introducing.
Henceforth, all decisions of cabinet will require the potential environmental effects to be assessed and considered. To help build public confidence that this is being done consistently and well, the responsible minister will be required to make a clear statement about the environmental effects of the policy initiative at the time it is announced. Also, to help ensure consistency and to enable the public to see the rules under which government is functioning in this regard, the Minister of the Environment has been asked to develop a set of clear guidelines for use by all departments, and the Privy Council Office has been asked to amend cabinet procedural manuals accordingly.
Further opportunity for public scrutiny can be reinforced by the House of Commons Standing Committee on the Environment which can request any minister to appear before it to explain the environmental implications of any new policy or any new program. The government will encourage and welcome this form of public accountability.
This is a great step forward. It is one which is virtually unprecedented in the world, let alone in Canada. We do not hide the fact that neither we nor any other country in the world have all the techniques fully developed for environment-economy integration in policies, but we are going to do it as well as it can be done and improve our techniques along the way. Leadership almost always requires breaking new ground. We have the strength and the resolve to do that.
A second vitally important element of our reform package is a consistent and predictable program of financial assistance to participants in public reviews that may be required in the process set out in Bill C-78 and, for that matter, any public reviews that may be undertaken under the present regime until Bill C-78 is able to be
June 26, 1990

implemented. This is going to be introduced, immediately after funds are approved by Treasury Board. We have learned over the years that whenever financial assistance is provided to review participants the issues are debated much more cogently and the results achieved are much more satisfying to all concerned.
The funding is usually directed as a matter of priority to communities and individuals most directly affected by a proposed development. This enables them to study and understand the issues thoroughly and to prepare well considered submissions to review panels. It minimizes antagonistic rhetoric and promotes useful dialogue.
For each public review the funds for this purpose will be allocated according to strict criteria and on the basis of applications submitted. Allocation decisions will be taken by special committees established for each review made up of credible individuals largely from outside government to help ensure independence. This again is almost unprecedented. The Netherlands, according to my understanding, is the only other country we know of that has a public review participant funding program. This will help build partnerships among decision makers and those affected by the decisions.
A third point I wish to raise at this time before returning to the details of the proposed legislation is a major international initiative the government intends to launch formally very soon to help increase awareness and action on environmental issues world-wide.
Canada, along with many other industrialized nations, provides a variety of forms of support, financial and otherwise, to goods and services exported abroad. To be consistent with its domestic policies, Canada must also consider the environmental effects of its actions affecting other countries. It does this formally with respect to bilateral aid initiatives and will continue to do so. To do this unilaterally with respect to export support actions would be highly unlikely to result in environmentally better decisions in the receiving countiy. What is more likely to happen is that Canadian exporters may not be able to compete effectively. In fact, it is probable that Canadian exporters may not even get invited to the bidding table if they are alone in carrying environmental demands.
An alternative course of action, and one which we believe is more likely to obtain environmental benefits
Government Orders
while not cutting off international markets for Canadian goods, is the development of an international accord in this area with the other countries in competition for the same export markets.
This has the potential to be of great international significance from an environmental point of view. While we cannot set a firm deadline for this process since that would pre-empt the negotiations, the government has requested that the Minister of the Environment and the Secretary of State for External Affairs report back to cabinet in three years on the progress made by that time. The expectation is that there would be substantial progress.
Mr. Speaker, as you can see, even though we know that Bill C-78 is a strong and comprehensive piece of environmental assessment legislation, we are not letting the matter rest there. The additional initiatives that I have outlined this morning demonstrate clearly to the Canadian people that this government is strongly and irrevocably committed to making all its decisions based on sound environmental criteria and to ensuring that the affected public has a fair opportunity and the means to influence those decisions.
I wish now to return to the bill itself. I would like to characterize the key features of the bill in order to give members an appreciation of the impressive advances it is introducing to the field of environmental assessment. Other government speakers during the course of this debate will certainly go into more detail about the process described in the bill. My intent is to touch on the highlights.
The stated purpose of Bill C-78 is to ensure that project decisions by responsible authorities are based on an informed appreciation of the likely environmental effects, to encourage project decisions by responsible authorities that promote and maintain a healthy environment and a healthy economy, to ensure that projects in Canada do not cause serious environmental effects outside the jurisdictions in which they are located.
This is in the context, as the bill itself states, of providing an "effective means of integrating environmental factors into planning and decision-making processes in a manner that ensures that present needs are met without compromising the ability to meet the needs of future generations". This is the concept of sustainable development that is the driving force behind this bill.

June 26, 1990
Government Orders
The bill requires government departments and agencies to give projects for which they have decision-making authority the degree of assessment warranted in the circumstances. If projects are determined to have no environmental relevance they will be excluded. It is important to note, however, that the bill is designed to have very broad application. Any exclusions require specific decisions based upon narrow criteria to avoid abuse.
All projects characterized in a list, which will be issued by regulation, as having potentially major environmental significance will be required to undergo mandatory environmental study and reporting. The Minister of the Environment will then make a decision as to whether a formal public review will be needed. All such mandatory environmental studies will entail consultation with the public and a review by government agencies with appropriate environmental expertise. It is anticipated that this provision will have a profound effect on the way developers interact with those potentially affected by development. They will have to start talking at an early stage to those affected in an effort to find mutually acceptable solutions to identified problems. Developers will want to do all they can to submit a mandatory environmental assessment report to the minister which identifies solutions, not just problems. Dialogue of this kind will improve, trust will build, and better solutions will emerge.
For other projects, that is those not on the list, an environmental screening will be required which may lead to a public review or to the project proceeding with appropriate mitigation measures.
If a public review is needed, the environment minister may choose between a mediation and a public review by a panel. In certain cases both may be needed.
A new agency will be created to administer the legislation and to advise the Minister of the Environment in the implementation of the process. The agency will be called the Canadian Environmental Assessment Agency and will be fully independent of Environment Canada, unlike the present federal Environmental Assessment Review Office.
A new provision is being introduced in this bill designed to safeguard the environment of one jurisdiction
from actions initiated in another. With this provision, if the trans-border environmental issue is serious and the parties have been unable to come to an accommodation regarding the way it should be assessed, the federal environment minister may require a federal review and may issue a stop work order on the project in question until the minister is satisfied that the trans-border environmental effects are acceptable. This is a potentially very important provision, not only because of the trans-border safeguard but also because it contains authority to protect certain lands of interest to Indian people which are not necessarily on designated reserves.
I would now like to summarize the important advances being made in Bill C-78 for the whole field of environmental assessment in Canada.
First, the Minister of the Environment makes the key process decisions regarding the need for a public review. This decision is currently taken by the minister responsible for the project and sometimes leads to accusations of the fox guarding the chicken coop. Bill C-78 places this responsibility where it belongs.
Second, all major projects must undergo mandatory assessment which must include public consultation. This is currently discretionary.
Third, assessments of major projects must include a consideration of cumulative environmental effects of the project relative to other projects affecting the same environment, alternative ways of carrying out the project, the reasons for proposing the project, and effects of the project on the sustainability for future generations of any renewable resources that might be affected by the project.
Each of these requirements on its own would be seen as very significant improvements. Taken together, the advance in my opinion is truly impressive.
Furthermore, public registries will be created and maintained for all assessed projects and will normally be located in the vicinity of the project so that those who might be affected by it can understand it and influence it.
Moreover, public review panels will be fully independent of government. Currently, although most members of panels are from outside government, the chairman or chairperson is a public servant. In the future the chair will also be from outside government.
June 26, 1990

Public review panels will have subpoena powers, enforceable by the Federal Court. Currently it is necessary to rely on the goodwill of participants, and from time to time not all useful information is made available.
A new provision will be introduced to enable appointment of a mediator to resolve environmental disputes when the conditions are right and when there is a willingness on the part of all key parties to find a solution.
All major projects will require the preparation of follow up and monitoring plans. Until now this has been one of the most significant deficiencies of environmental assessment processes everywhere in the world. To our knowledge, there are only two other countries in the world which allow for follow up. According to my understanding they are the Netherlands and the United States of America.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-78 today.
Unfortunately, it is a bill that fails on many tests. I will spend the next few minutes going through the history of how we got to where we are and why there will have to be substantive changes to the legislation if it is to be accepted widely by the Canadian public, as I think the government would like.
The federal environmental assessment and review process known as EARP was developed in response to a December, 1973 cabinet decision to provide for evaluation of environmentally significant undertakings subject to federal control. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, that was during a period of a minority government. In fact, we got some fairly good legislation under way during that period of time.
The main outlines of the process were approved by cabinet in April of 1974. Minor revisions were made by a cabinet directive in 1977. In its initial form EARP was entirely administrative. A 1979 amendment to the Government Organization Act gave EARP a statutory basis for the first time by authorizing the Minister of the Environment to establish and operate an environmental assessment process.
Since 1979 the federal Minister of the Environment's duties have included the following responsibility:
- to ensure that new federal projects, programs and activities are assessed early in the planning process for potential adverse effects on the quality of the natural environment and that a further review is carried out of those projects, programs and activities that are found to have probably significant adverse effects-
In 1983, following 10 years of experience with EARP, the federal cabinet ordered a formal evaluation of the program. This resulted in the proclamation of an Order in Council on June 22, 1984 under the Government Organization Act. This Order in Council replaced the previous cabinet directives that established the program.
It is that 1984 cabinet guidelines order upon which the Federal Court ruling was made on the Rafferty-Alame-da and the unanimous ruling of the Federal Court of Appeal on the Oldman.
The EARP guidelines order is applicable to any proposal that,
(a)	is to be undertaken by an initiating department;
(b)	that may have an environmental effect on an area of federal responsibility;
(c)	for which the government of Canada has a financial commitment; or
(d)	that is located on lands, including the offshore, that are administered by the Government of Canada.
It is on that 1984 cabinet guidelines order that many Canadians are waiting to obtain assurance from the Government of Canada prior to Parliament rising that the guidelines order will not be tampered with.
Since Bill C-78 is now moving through the House, I would hope that today the parliamentary secretary or someone in the cabinet would give an assurance that the guidelines order will not be tampered with as we await the passage and proclamation of C-78, a piece of legislation which I said requires some rather drastic modifications. Let me spend a few moments on that.
My friend who just spoke pointed out that the Conservative Party did promise during the 1984 election that some kind of EARP legislation would be brought forward soon. That was six years ago.

After a year of hearings in 1987-and I think this is germane because of these so-called Green Plan hearings that are going on-how may Canadians have an expectation that that process is actually going to produce some kind of useful and functioning environmental legislation and fiscal framework?

The press release of October 20, 1988 quoted the then environment minister, Tom McMillan, as saying: "We are prepared to subject every federal undertaking and every undertaking on federal lands to a thorough environmental impact study."

After three years in office it then had a year of hearings and then made promises for another two years. Finally it brought the legislation forward. The legislation has been gunny-bagged. Even the gunny-bagged legislation is not supposed to come in for another year and a half. One can only wonder how anything could possibly move that slowly, other than a slowly melting glacier.
The Ottawa Sun, on the day that the legislation was released, quoted my friend from Davenport as saying that the bill was a step in the right direction. A very timid step, Mr. Speaker. The Montreal Gazette went on to quote him as saying: "It deserves intensive and speedy study so we can make it the law of the land".
It certainly is going to require intensive work because the legislation is almost totally inadequate. It allows the government to get out of having due process on almost any project, no matter what the magnitude.
This legislation, as drafted, would not in its present draft apply to the largest industrial project ever proposed in the history of North America, James Bay II. This

June 26, 1990
Government Orders
legislation would not apply. It is discretionary. It will not apply to the largest industrial project which will flood 5,000 square kilometres of the province of Quebec, cause enormous methane releases to the atmosphere, wipe out the only freshwater seal population in the world, harm the whale populations in James Bay, divert many river systems so that they will flow in the opposite direction to which they already do and require the clear-cutting and the dumping of thousands of square miles of forests. This has been demonstrated in the March edition of Science Magazine as being the largest, single, carbon sink on planet earth, the northern boreal forest. It used to be thought that it was the oceans. Now, because of advances in science, we know it is the forests.
Amory Lovins appeared before the Standing Committee of Parliament, and the Canadian media did not even cover the fact that he had done a study for the northern tier states which showed that simply by revamping with new motors and with state of the art conservation and by redoing the buildings, the industry, and the homes only on the Island of Montreal, more power could be saved than would be generated by James Bay II. In fact, there would be an incremental bit of power that could be sold to the northern tier states at lower than the cost of any James Bay I power now available after almost a decade and a half of amortization.
The country is being led by a good chunk of the business community that can only be described from an environmental perspective as the lunatic fringe. In terms of their accounting procedures they completely exclude outside impacts on the environment. Pulp companies generate 40 per cent of the marine pollution in Canada. They consider the rivers, lakes, and oceans of Canada to be an open sewer for their free, uncosted benefit.
The atmosphere of planet earth is being considered as a gigantic garbage dump for those who want to dump acid precipitation. For those who want to move toxic and hazardous materials that they cannot take to a land fill, they put them in the atmosphere and they blow into another country, out on to the ocean, or out into the countryside.
Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, CFCs. The Minister of the Environment is in London and we have already had leaks. We understand the Canadian position is
substantially weaker than the all-party unanimous agreement on CFC and halon reduction. All three parties in this House are onside. The Minister of the Environment runs off to London to take a weaker position.
Who is his friend? Is it Dupont? Is it Allied Chemicals? Why would a minister not take the position which could only be described as a lowest common denominator? That report certainly did not represent the highest rate of reduction of CFCs and halons that we could possibly attain, but that is not being pursued.
This legislation has to be seen through the transparencies, the way it has been so carefully crafted that wherever there is strength there is a complete return of that power to the political level and wherever a particular project is seen as politically sensitive like the Rafferty-Alameda, even though it is wrong, even though it is contrary to the law, even though it is in violation of a court order, it still proceeds. Wink, wink, nudge, nudge; you know what I mean. The Prime Minister calls Grant: "Hi Grant, I won't get in your way. Don't worry. I know you are getting politically upset. Go with the project". "Oh, Mr. Getty, the Oldman. Go ahead. Just build it on safety. That is right. Construct it all the way, but before you drop the last grain of sand, stop, and we will study it and see whether or not it is good, bad or indifferent".
That is madness. We know too much about the environment now. We could well all perish within our own lifetimes because of some of the things that we are doing to the globe's environment.
Forty thousand children under the age of 12 will die today from starvation and preventable disease. Is anybody doing anything about it?
The cartoon that was run recently in The Regina Leader Post told it all: a picture of a small, shrivelled up, starving child reading about Earth Day and saying: "Oh, well, if they care as much about us as they do about the environment, will we all survive?"
With 40,000 a day starving to death, I somehow doubt these geniuses on the government side who say: "No, we cannot really go through all these screening processes. We really need to be able to keep our radioactive material, 100 million metric tons at Elliot Lake, unsafely. We really need to be able to dump all of our pulp mill pollution into the rivers".
June 26, 1990

To have not come forward at this point in the world's history, let alone Canada's history, without adequate environmental assessment legislation is a serious underestimation of what Canadians expect now of government.
The head of FEARO, Mr. Robinson went on in an interview with The Toronto Star, June 19, 1990, to talk about government departments being unable to agree whether reviews would affect their areas. He said: "Of course everyone is turf protecting". That is used as the reason the necessary pieces of legislation to trigger the activity of this legislation have been purposefully left out. The Minister of the Environment states that they will be included over time to make the legislation dynamic. Perhaps the minister should get out a thesaurus and find out what is the opposite of dynamic, because that is what this legislation is without that being included.
I think I have covered Rafferty and Oldman enough, but northerners are concerned about things like the impact of organochlorines, furans, and dioxin in the Peace and Athabasca rivers flowing up and particularly affecting their aquatic life, fish, birds, and so on.
What does this legislation do? Would there be an EARP triggered under this in relation to either a singular pulp mill in the province of Alberta or any other province or territory? The answer is no.
Would there be one triggered because of the cumulative impact of 5, 10, 15, or 20 pulp mills on the same systems? The answer is no.
Would there be one triggered because of the clear cutting of a third of the province of Alberta, 220,000 square kilometres, out from under the noses of Albertans? Would there be anything under this because of its potential impact on reducing the carbon fixing efficiency and capacity of a country like Canada? No.
What is this legislation, really? This is a public relations exercise, and it should not be seen as anything other than that.
What about west coast tanker traffic? We have had the Nestucca spill. We have had the Exxon Valdez. We have had spills in downtown Vancouver, right in the harbour.
Government Orders
Would there be a possibility of triggering an EARP under this one? No.
Could you even go to the courts to get a judicial review? Mr. Speaker, you only have to look in this legislation to find that only where there is extremely narrow grounds can you ever do what public interest groups have been doing in relation to the Oldman or the Rafferty-Alameda. We know why and I will come to that in a moment when I quote from the Bill Oppen memo, the famous Alberta memo about what the provinces wanted gutted from any legislation that would come before and through this House.
Would this do anything about global wanning? No. Ozone depletion? No. Acid rain? No. Great Lakes water quality? No. Arctic pollution? No. Poisoning of the belugas in the St. Lawrence? No. The loss of an acre of forests in Canada every five seconds? No.
What about the 20 per cent? In 1988 we had an international conference in Toronto and a scientific agreement suggesting that Canada and other countries would have a 20 per cent reduction from 1988 levels by the year 2005 in releases of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. That went too far. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources did not like that. When the former Minister of the Environment went to Bergen, he said that Canada would at least freeze carbon dioxide levels to the year 2000.1 understand he was promptly phoned by the PMO and told he had to eat those words.
It was not too long before he resigned. That again was the lowest common denominator. If we are not even going to freeze carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gas emissions into the atmosphere, life, at least human life, will not survive.
No one likes to talk in terms of that kind of fundamentally accepted scientific reality. People should read the IPCC, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. One thousand of the best known climatological scientists in the world have agreed that we need 60 per cent to 80 per cent reduction in all of the greenhouse gas families in order to stabilize the atmosphere.
What is this government doing? The greenhouse gas emissions, including CFCs, have gone up every single day, every single hour, every single month, every single year it has been in office, and it claims to be environmentally committed.

June 26, 1990
Government Orders
Let us take a look at what was said in this famous Alberta memo from Mr. Oppen, because he got just about everything that he wanted. This was a meeting in Vancouver that involved a number of provincial bureaucrats acting, I take it, on behalf of their ministers. Here are the sort of things they wanted.
There must be the capability through administrative agreements for Canada to defer to a provincial process.
That is very nice; just simply turn it over to the provinces.
The act, or the regulations, must contain an exclusion or grandfather clause for projects that are either under way or that have previously been reviewed.
They wanted that and they got that.
Reasonable time limits are to be imposed on reviews-This would only be appropriate in the case where a project is 100 per cent federal-The provinces need to be a party to the development of the exclusion and compulsory review lists.
That is part six and the soon to become famous 55(2) list. There will be lines with all of the Tory bag persons, I guess to put it properly, across the country saying: "Hey, how much to be a 55(2)?" They will be lining up to get on that exclusionary list. Certainly the provinces were very much in favour of that.
With respect to the interim measures, the provinces will demand that action be taken to amend the existing EARP Guidelines Order in order to remove environmental policy from the courts.
Well the provinces certainly got that.
Alberta has also asked that the issue of delegation of administration of the habitat and pollution provision of the Fisheries Act be considered within the context of these consultations as a related issue.
Some of the provinces even want federal legislation entirely turned over to them. It is not enough that they have a gutted and gutless act. They actually want the entire statutory and constitutional powers of Canada turned over to them.
What is missing? Let me quickly list it for you, Mr. Speaker. I know we are starting to run out of time, which is too bad because one could go on at some length about legislation that is so interesting, particularly because of its failures. However let me just make a few suggestions. These were suggestions made by Bill Andrews, Executive Director of the West Coast Environmental Law Association, regarding an earlier draft that came out, but they certainly still apply to this one.
I recommend that following points which are omitted from or mentioned but not supported in the subject document.
First, that the forthcoming legislation include a mechanism for environmental assessment of existing projects, policies, and programs. That is not there.
Second, the criteria for environmental assessment policies and programs be set by regulation with public input. There does not seem to be anything that would allow for that.
Third, that the Minister of the Environment be authorized to issue an environmental permit without which an activity subject to the environmental assessment process would not be able to proceed.
Fourth, that it be mandatory that a monitoring plan be included in an initial environmental evaluation or an environmental assessment report.
Fifth, that there be a provision for auditing of the monitoring that is conducted according to the environmental assessments.
Sixth, that there be a parliamentary commissioner on the environment to monitor the implementation of the environmental assessment process.
Seventh, that the legislation require that Crown corporations meet the environmental assessment standards applicable to other federal operations and that these corporations not have a special privilege to opt for a provincial environmental assessment process.
Eighth, that the primary decision on whether to send an activity to public review be taken by the Environmental Assessment Agency with an appeal to the Minister of the Environment.
Ninth, that there be a statutory provision for public input on draft agreements with provinces and other jurisdictions regarding environmental assessment procedures and standards prior to the finalization of these agreements.
Tenth, that the authority of a panel to impose costs against a proponent include expenses incurred by public participants in additional to those funded by the Environmental Assessment Agency.
Eleventh, that environmental assessments be imposed on federal spending on support for exports.
Twelfth, that the decision of the initiating department regarding whether or not to conduct an initial environ-

mental evaluation be subject to an appeal first to the Environmental Assessment Agency and then to the Minister of the Environment.
These all seem like 12 very logical recommendations that will have to be included in Bill C-78.
So one can see, Mr. Speaker, even in the few brief moments that I have had here this morning-and I know I have kept you spellbound-there is an awful lot of hard work to be done simply to drag Bill C-78 up out of the gutter where it got trampled by cabinet.
There was probably a fairly nice strategy and piece of legislation developed by Mr. Robinson and others who worked on this and spent $14 million studying how to create a stand alone environmental assessment process that would work.
Unfortunately cabinet came along, as I said, and said: "Let's get those statutes out of there". It jerked the Fisheries Act and everything else out and then said: "Well, the provinces don't ever want an Oldman or Rafferty-Alameda decision, so let's jerk that judicial access out of there. Now we have got to have an exclusionary list. There is no better way to get pulp companies and others on side than by developing this exclusionary list. It might cost you a few bucks to get on that list, but let's keep that trap door open". We have to close those trap doors.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The hon. member's time has expired.
It being one o'clock I do not leave the chair until two o'clock this day.
The House took recess at 1 p.m.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to stress the steadfast loyalty of the Hon. Brian Mulroney to Quebec. In the history of Quebec, he is the only prime minister of Canada who has defended
Quebec's constitutional interests with such energy and tenacity.
Meech is dead. We must look not to the past but to the future. We still have a lot to do.
An incredible consensus has developed among Quebec's political leaders and the people of Quebec. We must show our solidarity and work together to protect and promote Quebec's interests and the future of Canada.
Yesterday, Quebec celebrated its national holiday with dignity. Untold crowds of happy and proud Quebecers showed a solidarity never seen before. They expressed their pride in being Quebecers and they did so loud and clear. Mr. Speaker, there were more people on tie Sainte-Helene than on Prince Edward Island, more people on Sherbrooke street in Montreal than the entire population of Newfoundland.
Jean Chretien is hardly the man to ensure that Quebec's status is properly understood and that Quebec is recognized as a distinct society.

Saturday night at the Saddledome in Calgary, some 5,000 solid Liberals elected the Hon. Jean Chretien as Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada, on the first ballot.
Not long ago-in 1986-the Prime Minister of Canada said in this House the following about Jean Chretien, and I quote: "He loves Quebec, believes sincerely in Canada and has his own special way of expressing his feelings".
To people like me who believe in this beautiful country, this Canada of ours, he is a ray of hope. Thank you, Jean Chretien, and congratulations!

Mr. Speaker, on Thursday last a report was released about safety on the B.C. ferries. B.C. ferries carry more than 19 million passengers each year.
The report was prepared by a committee appointed both by the union and the corporation. The report unanimously condemned the Coast Guard for its complete failure to maintain safety practices on B.C. ferries.

June 26, 1990
The report pointed to the carrying of dangerous cargoes outside the rules, overcrowding of B.C. ferries, the resulting lack of safety equipment and the failure to have adequate training programs.
It is the job of Transport Canada and the Coast Guard to ensure the protection of passengers and crews on B.C. ferries. The reaction of the Coast Guard, through a Mr. Peter Booker, was first to say he had not read the report; second to say that 90 per cent of it was wrong; and third, to criticize the president of the B.C. Ferry Marine Workers for his comments.
Accordingly, I call on the government to take this report seriously and to act to protect the people of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to draw special attention to the Canadian Safety Council's eighteenth annual Farm Safety Week campaign which will take place from July 25 to July 31, 1990.
The Hon. Don Mazankowski is pleased to endorse the campaign which this year highlights the theme of farm machinery, safe operation, transport and maintenance and stresses- safe working habits on the farm.
Every year when man and machine interact in the farm workplace, there are fatalities and serious injuries which could be avoided, particularly those tractor-involved mishaps which account for about 70 per cent of all fatalities and injuries.
We commend the Canada Safety Council in its efforts to minimize serious accidents and to bring safety information to the attention of farming communities and agriculture-related businesses.
In invite members of the House to join with me in saluting farmers across the country for their hard work and vital contribution to Canada's well being.

Mr. Speaker, this government decided to blame Premier Wells for its
failure on the Meech Lake Accord rather than accept responsibility. The facts are that this government ignored, between 1987 and now, each and every recommendation to improve and correct the accord itself. As a result of such indifference the aboriginal people are left out of Canada's constitution. Imagine! This is not all. Millions of other Canadians are also left out.
Why blame Premier Wells? Because the Prime Minister desperately needs a scapegoat. Who is to be blamed when last Friday Senator Murray did not return the Premier's call? Why did the government reverse its position on the firmness of the deadline?
What this government hates to admit is the fact that the Meech Lake Accord died in the Manitoba legislature, where a courageous man, Elijah Harper, said no on behalf of the first people of Canada and on behalf of all those who believe that the first people must be in Canada's constitution.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to compete effectively in the global market-place, Canada requires a highly skilled, flexible and educated workforce.
To meet this demand there is a fundamental need to address the growing shortage of skilled workers. In my riding of Sarnia-Lambton, the Lambton Industrial Training Committee has taken up this challenge. Entitled "Skills OK", the committee has recently launched a well organized and thought provoking awareness campaign, including this very attractive T-shirt, that talks about about "Skills OK", promotes skilled occupations as desirable career goals for our youth, and the member for Kent could probably take advantage of this. "Skills OK" seeks to demonstrate that skilled trades should not be occupations entered into by default of other perceived better careers. Rather, these are more than simply jobs. They are important and worthy careers which, in themselves, are integral to the future economic growth and competitiveness of this country.
I salute the activities of the Lambton Industrial Training Committee and urge others to emulate their efforts.

June 26, 1990

Mr. Speaker, we saw recently what international pressure could do in a country like El Salvador, when President Cristiani rescinded his decision to privatize the university there.
What we would like to see beginning now is that same kind of international pressure with respect to the parliamentary elections which will be held in El Salvador in 1991. What I would like to do today, as a result of meetings that I have had with the MNR here in Canada and the trade union movement from El Salvador, is urge the government to devote as much resources as needed to ensure that the election in El Salvador is every bit as free and fair as the election that was held in Nicaragua.
I realize that the government in El Salvador is not as friendly to the notion of a free and fair election but, nevertheless, the international community and in this case Canada must show some leadership to begin providing the resources now to do the important pre-election work, as well as the election work, to ensure a free and fair election in El Salvador.

Mr. Speaker, on Saturday, Liberals from all across Canada made a clear choice, electing the Hon. Jean Chretien as Leader of the Liberal Party.
His first ballot victory is an indication from the party of the support for the vision he has for Canada. His experience as a parliamentarian, his patriotism as a Canadian and his strength as a leader are all welcomed by Canadians. Under the direction of the Hon. Jean Chretien, the Liberal Party will gain the strength, unity and vision to bring the Canadian family together.
We, as Liberals, are an open party representing Canadians from all walks of life. We encourage open dialogue and we debate one another with vigour, but our goal is always for a strong and united Canada that will stand together for our children and future generations. I believe that is the goal that the Hon. Jean Chretien, the new Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada, can now help us realize.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate Mr. Chretien personally for his victory at the Liberal leadership convention.
Mr. Speaker, I have something to say to the Liberal Premier of Newfoundland, Clyde Wells. I ask him why he betrayed his signature on the Meech Lake Accord, which he signed bn June 9, 1990.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw to the attention of the House three members of the cabinet of the Republic of Croatia. The new cabinet was sworn in on May 30, 1990, the result of the first free election in post-war history. On that occasion there were six members of Parliament, from all sides of the House, who went to Croatia to observe the elections.
In the gallery today is Mr. Manolic, who is a member of the Presidency; Dr. M. Babic, who is Vice-President; and Mr. G. Susak, who is Minister of Immigration.
On behalf of the House, Mr. Speaker, we welcome them to Canada and wish the Republic of Croatia all the best.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-21 is a bill designed to do many things, not the least of which is to provide for an opportunity for mothers and fathers to be with their newborn infants for a period of up to 30 weeks.
Why is the Senate not passing this bill? Does the Senate have a problem with this legislation? Are members of the the Senate not sensitive to this problem because they are not capable of becoming new parents? Do they not believe in the importance of the family and essentially the importance of the opportunity for a child

Oral Questions
to develop a close relationship with its parents in the first few months of its life?
I assume the answer is no, to all of the above. I assume that the Senate is saying no to all new parents in Canada. Prospective parents in Canada deplore this insensitive non-action and I personally find the Senate's non-action despicable.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last weekend in Calgary, Liberals from right across this great land had their leadership convention and chose the Hon. Jean Chretien as their new leader.
Here is what one well-known Canadian said about Jean Chretien, "-a great Quebecer and a great Canadian, a brave and dedicated member, the extremely likeable man who made an unforgettable impression on all Canadians, a witty and compassionate person. He loves Quebec and believes deeply in Canada and has a unique and thoughtful way of expressing that".
Who said that?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: All right, it was the member for Charlevoix, the right hon. Prime Minister who said that.

Mr. Speaker, as it happened, the day after Meech failed, the people of Quebec took to the streets to celebrate their national holiday.
Yesterday's incredible demonstration where they marched towards their destiny and their future, with or without Canadian partners, was also a message from Quebecers to their political leaders.
They thanked the Prime Minister of Canada for doing his utmost, right to the end, to defend the aspirations of Quebec with honour and dignity.
To Jean Chretien and his mentor, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, and his acolytes Carstairs and Wells, Quebec gave the following warning: It will remember for a long time, indeed forever, that they were the ones who really buried the Meech Lake Accord.

And as the new leader of the Liberal Party rightly said, "We have a lot of work to do".

Mr. Speaker, what was once known as the forgotten war was nationally remembered on Sunday when hundreds of Canadians gathered at the National War Memorial and at cenotaphs across Canada to mark the fortieth anniversary of the outbreak of the Korean war. The veterans of the Korean war, just like those who served in the First and Second World Wars, were certainly being remembered in practical terms by this government.
Let us recall the good news announced just this month by the Minister of Veterans Affairs, an agreement for 200 long-term hospital beds in British Columbia, services under the Veterans Independence Program for one year for spouses of deceased veterans, increased income protection for spouses of veterans in long-term care institutions, the payment of interest for the first time on trust funds administered by Veterans Affairs, special trusts for needy veterans, payments of attendants' allowances for one year to spouses of certain veterans and, finally, the raising of the ceiling for funeral assistance.
The Canadian men and women who served in Korea deserve programs and benefits which are second to none in the world and this government is delivering.

Mr. Speaker, next Sunday, we celebrate our 123rd anniversary as a country. Let us take the time to appreciate what we have been, what we are, what we can become.

There are many older countries that are just starting to appreciate some of the fundamental rights and freedoms that we have now. For example, with the crumbling of the wall between the two Germanys, East Germany taking its first real step toward democracy. The release of Nelson Mandela is a significant gesture toward human rights and racial equality.

June 26, 1990

Canada is indeed at a critical time in its history, but let us celebrate what we share as a people: our people, our rich resources, our fundamental rights and freedoms, our diverse cultures, our reputation for tolerance not only at home but abroad, and our ability to improve what we have built together thus far. Let us celebrate what we are and what we can be.

Let us all celebrate together!

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the efforts of a group of citizens in my riding of Cariboo-Chilcotin. These ordinary citizens from Quesnel, B.C., have launched a group called MEND-the Movement to End National Disunity-in an attempt to promote friendship between all Canadians.
The group has already organized a public conference call between elementary schools from each of our provinces and territories involving over 3,000 students. Petitions have been collected. Letters of support have been written by schools and church and business groups to their Quebec counterparts, offering hands of friendship.
These people themselves cannot solve the problem of national unity, but their love of their country and for all of their fellow Canadians serves to remind us that it is ordinary Canadians who built this country and it is ordinary Canadians who remain its greatest asset.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
Hear, hear.

I thank my colleagues for their applause but I direct their attention to the statement made by the Deputy Whip confirming the results of the leadership convention last week and the kind words spoken by the Prime Minister about our new leader some years ago.

Hear, hear.
Oral Questions

I have a question for the Prime Minister. In his speech to the nation on television last Saturday regarding the failure of the Constitutional Accord of 1987, the Prime Minister said: "It is a time to mend divisions, and heal wounds, and reach out to fellow Canadians." Those are the words of the Prime Minister on national television last Saturday.
However, this morning the Liberal House leader was informed that the government did not intend to call the Hibernia legislation for report stage and third and final reading today, or at any time this week, even though the House is going to adjourn this Friday until September.
How does it fit in with the Prime Minister's desire to heal wounds, mend divisions, and reach out to Canadians by stalling on an important economic project with major industrial benefits for Newfoundland, Quebec, and all of Canada?
Will the government call this Hibernia legislation for third and final reading today? If it does so, I assure the government that it will have the co-operation of the Official Opposition in passing this legislation immediately in the interests of Newfoundland, Quebec, and all of Canada. Will the government undertake this act of nation-building today?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the last week prior to the summer adjournment and there is an understandable desire by members on all sides of the House to leave and go back to their constituencies as soon as possible. I naturally consulted my colleagues as to what their needs were in terms of priorities for the summer agenda.
The Minister of Energy informed me that, in fact, the discussions and negotiations with regard to Hibernia were in no way conditional upon this legislation going through all three final stages.
The EARP legislation which we started today is very important. The amendments to the Parliament of Canada Act are very important. If we can get those two, we can do what Opposition members, our members, and members of the New Democratic Party would like, namely, to adjourn for the summer.

Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the government that as far as the Official Opposition is concerned, we are quite ready to stay here and pass this legislation because we think it is important as an act of nation building for Newfoundland, Quebec, and all of Canada. We regret that according to the Minister of Energy it is not one of the priorities of the government.

June 26, 1990
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week, in an attempt to save the 1987 Accord, the Prime Minister sent Senator Murray to meet aboriginal leaders in Manitoba with a six-point program to respond to their concerns.
I want to ask the Prime Minister whether he intends to continue the healing process by reaching out to aboriginals and implementing those points in the program for which constitutional negotiations and amendments are not necessary.
Would he agree this is important in order to end dissension, heal wounds and reach out to this very important group of Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition knows perfectly well that, before and during the negotiations on the Meech Lake Accord, there were many meetings with the aboriginal peoples on a bilateral basis between the Government of Canada and their representatives, and I want to give the House and the country the assurance that there will be many more. We have a number of bilateral problems to resolve, and we will do everything in our power to see to it that a settlement is reached that is fair and equitable to the aboriginal peoples.
It is truly unfortunate that the constitutional process provided by the Meech Lake Accord for aboriginal peoples no longer stands, as a result of the decision by one of the provinces last week not to proceed with a vote on the Meech Lake Accord. However, we will nevertheless meet, on a regular and satisfying basis, with aboriginal leaders in order to promote greater social justice for this constituency.

The Leader of the Opposition began by referring to some kind words that I apparently had for Mr. Chretien some years ago. He need not have looked back that far. On Sunday, I wrote the following to Mr. Chretien:
I wish to offer my sincere congratulations to the Honourable Jean
Chretien, on his election as Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada.
I offer Mr. Chretien my full co-operation in the important duties
he assumes today in Canada's democratic life.
Mila joins me in wishing happiness and good health to Mr. and
Mrs. Chretien and their family.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the words in the Prime Minister's statement are obviously most welcome.
If the Prime Minister will not allow the House to reach a final decision-if not today, then before the end of the week-on the Hibernia legislation and, specifically, if he will not undertake to put into effect those items in the six-point program he offered the native leaders in Manitoba that do not require constitutional amendment, then how can Canadians take the Prime Minister seriously when he says he wants to mend wounds, heal divisions, and reach out to Canadians? Does the Prime Minister's attitude not mean that many Canadians are right when they say that the Prime Minister has lost the moral authority to govern and should act accordingly?

Mr. Speaker, I know that some people, including my hon. friend, have made such elegant comments as those he has just repeated.
It will be for the people of Canada-

-for the people of Quebec and of Canada to judge at an appropriate time-

-to decide at an appropriate time who stood for Quebec's interests and who stood for the interests of a united Canada.
Hear, hear!
Let's have an election.

The hon. member from Toronto says: "Let's have an election". The last time he said that was in August of 1988 and look what happened.
The problem with the point of view that my hon. friend puts forward is that in Newfoundland the vote is not allowed in some areas.
Oh, oh.

I just want to say to the Leader of the Opposition that he will hear no criticism from me. All he has to do is hear the, comments made by the hon. member for LaSalle-Emard and members of his own caucus in regard to an important position that was not taken in the last week. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.

So today, we will maintain this tradition of bilateral negotiations which in the past twenty years or so, as I was saying, has resulted in a series of agreements with six or seven provinces involving issues of immigration and integrating immigrants into a new environment and so on.
It is in that context that we have been negotiating with the Government of Quebec for a long time now.

Mr. Speaker, in the spirit of the bilateral negotiations that the Prime Minister is referring to, on June 18 the federal government made an offer to the aboriginal people which included six various points. Tribal Council in British Columbia. I believe that is what he stated. Yet it was negotiations undertaken by this government which led to the framework agreement on the comprehensive land claim with the Nishga Tribal Council in July of 1989.

that week, that there was a method for extending the time for ratification?

undertake to submit the Constitution Amendment, 1987 for
appropriate legislative or public consideration and to use every
possible effort to achieve decision prior to June 23, 1990.
It is signed by Clyde Wells, Premier of Newfoundland and Labrador.

My Speaker, why did the Prime Minister not tell the First Ministers that he had a gimmick in reserve for giving them more time? If more time was available for Manitoba under this novel legal argument, why was there not more time available for the province of Newfoundland and Labrador?
If last Thursday he could find a way of rolling the deadline back from the period of Saskatchewan's ratification to September 23, why could that extension not be sought even today at the Supreme Court of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I am a little perplexed by my hon. friend's suggestion that perhaps more time was needed in Newfoundland and Labrador.
In point of fact, if he will consult the transcripts he will see that Premier Peterson of Ontario, Premier Devine of Saskatchewan, Premier McKenna of New Brunswick and I as Prime Minister of Canada went down and spoke to the Newfoundland legislature on the formal promise of the Premier of Newfoundland and Labrador that a vote would take place Thursday night or Friday morning, and it did not take place.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. A few weeks ago, the Minister of Finance stated that high interest rates in this country were partly a result of the constitutional impasse.
I now have the following question for the minister: Could he inform the House whether his government intends to pursue its monetary policy that keeps interest rates and the Canadian dollar at levels that are too high, a situation that is be coming very dangerous for the Canadian economy?

Mr. Speaker, I indicated some two or three weeks ago that there was a risk premium that was built into interest rates because of the uncertainty surrounding the Meech Lake Accord. That was a matter of fact at the time. That uncertainty is still there. There is still a risk premium, I would imagine, in the level of interest rates today.
I have said on a number of occasions that the more important reason for the level of interest rates that we are experiencing today is the level of inflationary pressure in the economy. Until we get that inflationary pressure out, we will have to endure these higher interest rates for a somewhat longer period of time.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Finance. In view of the minister's answer and in view of the fact that in the February budget the prediction for an average annual interest rate during 1990 was somewhere around 11 per cent-the fact is interest rates now are nearly 14 per cent-does the Minister of Finance not believe that the time has now come, in view of economic and constitutional reality in Canada, to either bring in a revised budget or to bring in a new budget based on the facts?

Mr. Speaker, I answered that question on numerous occasions in the House, a number of times when asked by the hon. member himself.
I indicated that there are offsetting factors here. Our revenues in 1989-90 were higher than expected, so we are going into fiscal year 1990-91 with a higher level of income and a higher level of revenues for the Government of Canada. There is an offset against the higher costs from our higher interest rates.
June 26, 1990

We are watching this on an ongoing basis. If it is appropriate to have some mid-term correction, we are prepared to take that action.

CHANGE OF AFFILIATION OF MEMBER FOR LONGUEUIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I entered federal politics for the first time in 1984, and I renewed my commitment in 1988.
I did so, first and foremost, in order to take an active part in implementing one of the most important proposals in Quebec's history. I did so because I was convinced I was taking part in a noble enterprise. I did so because I sincerely felt that it was possible to bring Quebec back into the constitutional family with honour and enthusiasm.

June 26, 1990
House of Commons
Like many other Quebecers, I was convinced that the Meech-Langevin Accord was an important first step, a step with which I could agree, despite certain concerns. I was convinced it was one step towards a flexible constitutional formula under which Quebec would be able to grow and prosper.
However, as recent events have borne out, this was not to be, despite the fact that we all placed our trust in this process and devoted all our energies and enthusiasm to this cause, with honesty and sincerity.
In this respect, we all know that the Prime Minister has shown extraordinary courage and energy. He has our respect and admiration, that goes without saying.
Only those who, at this critical point in our history, insist on engaging in petty politics refuse to recognize this fact. To those who think that someday they will govern Canada on the basis of an obsolete vision of this country, I say that Quebec's motto is: Je me souviens.
Today, I think it is clear that the process agreed on in 1987 cannot produce satisfactory results either for Quebec or Canada. It is simply impossible, because of the political and constitutional context we have inherited.
We must seek another way.
As a Quebecer, I am convinced this new way must first of all be defined by Quebecers, based on the interests of the people of Quebec.
I think this is the only feasible formula for considering a new form of participation in the Canadian federation. To be viable and satisfactory, however, it must be a different federation. It must be based on the participation of groups reflecting the many realities of Quebec and of Canada's regions.
That is why I feel obliged to resign from the caucus of the Progressive Conservative Party, and from now on, sit as an independent member. As such, I will be in a better position to act in a manner that is consistent with my initial commitment and to defend the interests of Quebecers in Ottawa.
At this point, I wish to thank the Prime Minister and congratulate him on his courage and perseverance. I want to say that I was proud to be a member of his team and to work for this fine and noble cause.
I can also assure him of my support for efforts and initiatives that are a response to the needs and aspirations of Quebec.
To my colleagues I want to say: I appreciated this chance to work with you, and I will continue to do so, if you wish, in order to promote the interests of Quebec in Ottawa.

subtopic: CHANGE OF AFFILIATION OF MEMBER FOR SHEFFORD
CHANGE OF AFFILIATION OF MEMBER FOR SHEFFORD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had the honour and privilege of representing the people of Shefford in this House for over ten years, and never did I have to qualify or question my loyalty towards Quebec or Canada. Nor did I ever have to question my loyalty towards the Liberal Party of Canada in the past ten years. Yet today, as a Quebecer, I find myself at a crossroads. As a Liberal I also find myself at a crossroads. During all those years since the Quebec referendum I believed it was possible to achieve renewed federalism within the existing institutions.
And during all those years, Mr. Speaker, I believed that the Liberal Party of Canada was the natural bridge between our country's two linguistic communities.
Mr. Speaker, my motivation and my commitment stem from the speech delivered by Pierre Elliott Trudeau on May 15,1980 at the Paul Sauve Arena. I felt bound by his solemn commitment towards Quebecers, and I should like to repeat those words which were so important in my career and for the destiny of Quebecers.
On May 15, 1980 Mr. Trudeau said: "We will not stop until it is achieved". He was referring to constitutional renewal. "If it is no, we all said it will be interpreted as a mandate for constitutional change and renewed federalism". He said: "I am not the only one saying this, so do the 74 Liberal members in Ottawa"-including me-"and the premiers of the other nine provinces. We will tell Canadians in the other provinces that we will not accept that the no be interpreted as an indication that everything is going fine and that things can remain as before. We want a change and we are putting our seats on the line to have that change".

Mr. Speaker, not only did I put my seat on the line, I put my youth, my energy and whatever talent God gave me to work towards the renewal of the federation and to achieve this dream which was shared by so many Quebecers.
I was very active in 1981-82 when the Constitution was patriated, believing as I did that it was the first step towards genuine renewed federalism. I soon realized that the work was incomplete because Quebec had been left aside.
In 1985, Mr. Speaker, when Robert Bourassa was elected, a federalist premier, at the same time as the Prime Minister across the aisle had been in office for a few years, the Quebec-Ottawa axis was finally free, finally open. And today, Mr. Speaker, I acknowledge that the Prime Minister is an ally of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, today I feel sad, humiliated and betrayed.

I said sad, humiliated and betrayed. For those who thought that Meech was too much, take note that from now on it is not enough.

Mr. Speaker, beginning today and henceforth I want to support Quebec's endeavour and play a role in the new scenario which will automatically follow the demise of the Meech Lake Accord. With my fellow citizens in Quebec, I want to take part in the definition of a comprehensive collective project.
