The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. de Cotret that Bill C-78, an Act to establish a federal environmental assessment process, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak to Bill C-78, an Act to establish a federal environmental assessment process, at second reading.

I want to continue with the debate this afternoon on Bill C-78. Opposition critics were very quick to find fault with this legislation when it was tabled in the House of Commons for first reading on June 18, 1990.
Government Orders
The NDP environment critic even had the temerity to suggest that the legislation was as full of holes as Swiss cheese.
Rather than find fault with the hon. member's bad taste, I would prefer to thank him for his analogy. After all, Mr. Speaker, Swiss is a world-class cheese and so too is Bill C-78 a world-class environmental assessment bill.
In my remarks to the House today I would like to focus on the scope of this bill in order to put to rest any concern that this legislation might be a retreat from the current guideline order. Nothing could be further from the truth.
This government is bringing forward legislation designed to bind government decision-making in a way that will ensure that every minister becomes, in addition to his or her regular responsibilities, an environment minister.
In such circumstances, a government that was less than fully committed to the environment might have sought to limit the scope of this legislation so as to leave its decision-making largely unfettered. Such has most assuredly not been the case with Bill C-78. This is a bill that is designed to expand the scope of the current environmental assessment process, not to restrict it.
This government is fully aware of the importance of the environment to Canadians. It is committed to protecting and maintaining environmental quality in all parts of Canada. The Canadian environmental assessment act will apply to virtually every project in which the federal government has an interest or an involvement. It will ensure that the environmental effects of all federal projects are fully understood before final decisions on whether or how to proceed with them are made.
The very broad scope of this legislation makes it abundantly clear that this government is prepared to leave no stone unturned in its efforts to bring a profound environmental ethic to all of its decisions and to all of its actions.
The scope of Bill C-78 is established right at the outset with the definitions of "environment", "environmental effect", and "projects".
Bill C-78 defines the environment as encompassing all of the components of the Earth including land, water and air as well as all layers of the atmosphere, all organic, and inorganic matter and living organisms, and

June 26, 1990
Government Orders
the interacting natural systems that we commonly refer to as the ecosystems.
This definition of environment not only provides the broadest possible scope for environmental assessment, it also recognizes that all natural systems are inter-related, thereby setting the stage for the theme of sustainable development which is evident throughout the legislation.
The second definition of critical importance to the scope of this legislation is environmental effect. Bill C-78 defines environmental effect as any change that a project may cause in the environment, as well as any effect that the environment may cause in a project. But the definition does not stop there. It goes on to make it clear that the consideration of such effects is not restricted to those that may occur in Canada, but it is also to include those that may occur outside Canada.
Even further, environmental effects will not stop with the environment, but are to include the effects of environmental change or damage on related health and socio-economic conditions. That means on people. Again it can be seen that this legislation is intended to have a very wide scope indeed.
The third and most important definition relating to the scope of environmental assessment is that of project. Bill C-78 defines a project as any physical work or physical activity that a proponent proposes to carry out.
This definition includes the construction, operation, modification, decommissioning, and abandonment of physical works such as factories, dams or pulp and paper mills, and the undertaking of physical activities such as low-level military flight training, for example. Clearly, the scope of the legislation is impressive, as should be obvious even to my hon. friends sitting opposite.
While definitions are an important element of any legislation, the real measure of the scope of application of the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act is to be found in the body of the legislation. Clause 5 of the bill outlines the cases where an environmental assessment of a project will be required. I would like to take a few minutes to describe the types of projects to which this legislation will apply because it is important that the House have a good appreciation of just how comprehensive the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act really is.
The act will apply to any project for which the federal government is a proponent. Such projects would include the fixed link to Prince Edward Island from New Brunswick, the north warning system in the high Arctic, and the possible expansion of Pearson International Airport at Toronto.
The act will apply to any project for which the federal government makes or authorizes payments, provides a guarantee for a loan, or provides any other form of financial assistance other than by means of general taxation measures. Such projects would include major offshore oil and gas developments, projects funded through regional development programs such as the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency or Western Economic Diversification, and foreign projects sponsored and supported by the Canadian International Development Agency.
The act will apply to any project for which the federal government sells, leases, transfers, or otherwise disposes of Crown lands. Such projects would include those that take place in Canada's offshore frontiers, those that take place on territorial lands in the North, and those that take place in national parks and on military reserves.
Finally, the act will apply to the issuance of permits and licences and the granting of approvals under various federal statutes and regulations which have the authority to deal effectively with the environmental effects of projects. These statues and regulations will be listed in a regulation made pursuant to the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act. The Minister of the Environment has already indicated that this list will include appropriate provisions for such statutes as the National Energy Board Act, the Railway Act, the Railway Relocation and Crossing Act, the Atomic Energy Control Act, the International River Improvements Act, the Fisheries Act, the National Parks Act, and the Canada Oil and Gas Act.
The Federal Environmental Assessment Review Office is currently undertaking a thorough review of all federal legislation having environmental powers with the intention of proposing an expanded list by the time that the legislative committee begins its clause-by-clause review of this bill. In addition, it is the intent of the government to add to this list on a continuing basis as new legislation is passed and current legislation is
June 26, 1990

amended and updated. It is for that reason that the list will be established by means of a regulation rather than as a schedule to the act.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, it will be the rare project falling within the purview of the federal government that is not subject to a very thorough environmental assessment before the federal government makes its final decisions.
To this point, I have focused my comments on the definitions and the types of projects that will be subject to the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act. While these have painted a very impressive picture of the scope of the legislation, I would also like to say a few words about the broad scope of the environmental assessment process itself. I would particularly like to emphasize that it is in this area that very substantial improvements have been made to the current guidelines order that this legislation is intended to replace.
In the current guidelines order, the scope of the environmental assessment process is restricted to the environmental effects of projects, any directly related social effects, and to the concerns of the public. In special cases under the guidelines, where the Minister of the Environment and the minister of the initiating department consider it appropriate, an environmental assessment may also include a consideration of the general socioeconomic effects of and the need for the project.
Let me turn, by comparison, to the scope of the environmental assessment process in the proposed legislation. When I finish describing this new process, I will defy anyone, including my friends opposite, to tell me that Bill C-78 is a retreat from the current situation. Instead, I will challenge my hon. friends on the other side of the House to open their minds, recognize the facts, and admit that this legislation represents a substantial improvement over the current process.
Clause 11 of Bill C-78 describes the factors that must be considered in conducting an environment assessment of a project. These are divided into two groups: those factors that must be considered in any project assessment, and those factors that must be considered in the
Government Orders
case of projects that are subject to a mandatory study, a panel review, or a mediation.
The environmental assessment of any project must, at the very least, include a consideration of four critical factors. The first of these factors is the environmental effects of the project. But this factor does not stop there, as it does under the current guidelines order. A consideration of the environmental effects of a project under the new legislation must include a consideration of the effects of any malfunctions or accidents that may occur in connection with the project. It must also include a consideration of any cumulative effects that are likely to result from the project in combination with other projects that are being carried out, or are likely to be carried out in the same vicinity.
This single factor alone represents a substantial improvement and a substantial broadening of the scope of environmental assessment relative to the current situation. For the first time, explicit recognition will be given to the fact that projects are subject to both mechanical failure and human error. Proponents will be required to build such considerations into their project plans in a manner that will anticipate the occurrence of malfunctions and accidents and prevent their effects from being felt in the environment.
Also for the first time, explicit recognition will be given to the fact that projects do not occur in environmental isolation, but can contribute, in a cumulative manner, to an over-all reduction of environmental quality. Proponents will be required to examine the environmental effects of their projects, both on their own merits and in relation to other existing and planned projects in the vicinity. In this manner, it will be possible for the first time to ensure the achievement of effective environmental quality goals and objectives.
The second of the four basic factors is the significance of any environmental effects that are likely to occur as a result of a project. A determination of the degree of significance will allow project proponents and federal authorities to focus their efforts on those effects which pose the greatest danger to the environment and on those measures that can most effectively reduce or eliminate those effects. In this manner, environmental

June 26, 1990
Government Orders
assessment will move from a subjective hit-and-miss art to an objective and cost-effective science.
The third of the four basic factors in environmental assessment under the new legislation pertains to the comments and concerns of the public. While this factor is similar to the one under the existing guidelines, the way in which this factor operates under the new legislation will be much improved. Bill C-78 provides far more numerous and more structured opportunities for the public to receive environmental assessment information and to participate in the environmental assessments of projects that are subject to the legislation. In short, the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act will establish a far more user-friendly process than the current guidelines order.
The final of the four basic factors that must be considered in the environmental assessment of any project is mitigation. There would be little sense in anticipating the environmental effects of a project if there was not a parallel requirement to take the necessary steps to control or eliminate those effects. The new Canadian Environmental Assessment Act will ensure that the proper mitigation measures are considered during the planning stages of projects and that effective measures are put in place at the start so that projects are safe from the time they are undertaken.
In short, the government is committed to anticipating and preventing environmental damage, rather than reacting to and curing, or attempting to cure, damage that has already occurred. This principle lies at the base of the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act and it makes infinitely good economic as well as environmental sense.
Those are the four basic factors that must be taken into consideration in the environmental assessment of any project under the proposed act. Impressive though they may be, they are not sufficient to achieve effectively the goal of sustainable development. Therefore, for major projects that will require a mandatory study, a panel review or a mediation, four additional factors will have to be considered.
The first is the purpose of the project. It will be important, in considering the environmental implications, to have a good appreciation of the need for and the advantages to be gained from that project.
The second additional factor for major projects is a consideration of alternative means of carrying out the project. It is often a fact that the most economical way of carrying out a project may be very environmentally damaging, and the most environmentally friendly way of carrying out a project may seem to be very costly. Alternatives must be considered.
The third additional factor for the environmental assessment of major projects is follow-up programs. In particular, emphasis will be placed on verifying the accuracy of the environmental assessment and determining the effectiveness of measures taken to mitigate the environmental effects of the project.
The final factor which must be considered is far from the least. It is a consideration of the short or long-term capacity for the regeneration of renewable resources that are likely to be significantly affected by a project.

As you know, Mr. Speaker, this government undertook a long time ago to honour its commitment to sustainable development as proposed in the 1987 report of the World Commission on Environment and Development, also known as the Brundtland Commission.
With the promulgation of the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, this commitment will take on a meaning that will extend its application to all major projects the government is involved in.
In this way, Mr. Speaker, we are living up to our commitment to make Canada, by the year 2000, the world's most environmentally friendly country.

In conclusion, since Bill C-78 was tabled on June 18,1 have been appalled by some of the statements attributed to supposedly informed environmental activists and opposition critics. These people have been very quick to offer their opinions on the scope of the legislation and to
June 26, 1990

suggest that the legislation represents a significant step backward from the current guidelines order. Nothing could be further from the truth.
The Canadian Environmental Assessment Act represents a bold initiative in the field of environmental assessment that will place Canada at the leading edge of responsible environmental stewardship. It represents a very significant expansion and improvement to the current guidelines Order in Council, and I trust that my remarks in the House today on the scope of the new process will put to rest any concerns in that regard.
Bill C-78 is a critically important legislative initiative that will provide environmental and economic benefits to Canadians for years to come and will place Canada in the forefront of economically concerned countries by the year 2,000.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your interest in and attention to this bill which is so important for our country.

that perhaps is too narrow or not comprehensive enough.

Mr. Speaker, I feel there is no process so clearly accountable than is the cabinet process of government. Frankly, it seems to me that the implications of our environmental assessment activity will be made clear to the public, and will be subject to public examination.
As a matter of fact, the bill conveys a very solid, strong commitment to full public participation. That is one of the principal criteria of the act. Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to speak today on Bill C-78, an act to establish the federal environmental assessment process.
It has been a long time coming, Mr. Speaker, and the Minister of the Environment has certainly produced a document of great effort, with the best of intentions, but I am afraid that it has clearly fallen short of the expectations of most Canadians who have been making demands for decisive environmental assessment legislation.
June 26, 1990

The Minister of the Environment is taking Canadians for fools if he thinks he is going to pacify us with yet another generalized framework of legislation. After three years of study and 15 drafts, the minister has provided us with environmental assessment legislation that is skeletal and without solidity, not what this country needs at this crucial point in the environmental health of our nation.
Canadians have been waiting for new environmental legislation that will replace the old informal guidelines we have been following aimlessly since 1984. This legislation had previously given the Tory cabinet broad latitude in which it has woven a tangled web of misused and ignored guidelines.
Once again, the government has cleverly slipped out of making any real decisions by simply deferring the bulk of the legislation, to be drafted at a later date. This could be two years down the road. This is time that we do not have in our battle to prevent the environmental destruction that is plaguing our country.
As I read through Bill C-78, I noted that it might strengthen guidelines that allow environmental impact studies on projects such as dams, pulp mills, navigable waters or nuclear power plants. I had hoped it might give force to the idea of sustainable development, taking into consideration perhaps industry studied depletion of our renewable resources and the cumulative effect of many concentrated industries.
I am left realizing, however, that there are several weaknesses inherent in this environmental assessment bill and there are many questions that are not strategically answered within. This bill has been purposely designed to avoid telling the public the critical and most important detail of how the government will go about regulating a project. The scope and essence of this bill have been lost because no clear regulations have been set out for us within the legislation.
Once again, we have a loose framework with regulations to be decided upon later in the game by public policy bureaucrats. Does it not make sense that these regulations should be made clear to everyone from the outset? What kind of game is the government playing with the environment when upcoming and developing projects have to deal with random regulations? The rules
Government Orders
are being made up as we go along and that is not playing fair with Canadians.
The Minister of the Environment hails this bill "as powerful in its impact on decision making". I question this line of thinking. The legislation will be worth nothing if cabinet fails to pass regulations listing all specific federal jurisdictions and legislation under which it can be used. Surely the people of Canada cannot be expected to blindly trust the cabinet to establish powers which will only be made public after the bill passes through the House of Commons, any time in the next two years or more.
There is a lack of strength of the environmental assessment agency process within the legislation. After reviewing a study of a particular project and the board finds it to present a risk, the agency can advise the environment minister to direct a panel of outside experts to assess that scheme.
The process starts off with good intentions, but then weakens. This panel could only make recommendations. It could not order a stop to any project. On top of there being a set of regulations to implement, the panel must make its recommendations, not to the environment minister or to the cabinet, but to the minister who wanted the project built in the first place. I see this as a waste of valuable study time. It is a process which seems to be defeating its own original purpose.
One of the government's own officials who helped draw up the bill, openly admits to this weakness, saying that the sponsoring minister may ignore the appointed panel and go ahead with the project. The only mechanism in place to prevent this from happening would be a mere appeal to the cabinet from the environment minister.
We have seen a similar process take place over the past 15 months in the case of the Green Plan. What did we end up with after an appeal from the former environmental minister? Nothing but a paltry framework for discussion. There is no solidity to the Green Plan, and now it seems there is no solidity to Bill C-78.
This legislation is not precise enough. It does not say how extensive the cabinet assessment must be, what standards for environmental protection must be followed, or how much of the cabinet assessment must be made public. Canadians must be wary of the existence of strong forces which we all know are pushing hard to

June 26, 1990
Government Orders
weaken any guidelines, so that the courts cannot intervene in federal projects.
This bill lacks strong enough mechanisms to ensure compliance with the rules that government sets out to ensure the proper quality of assessment be given within the project assessment of the bill. For a policy assessment to succeed, a mechanism with teeth needs to be entrenched within the project assessment, that being the part which is entrenched in the law. Right now, we do not have this.
Perhaps the government could consider appointing a commissioner of the environment who would act in a similar manner as the Office of the Commissioner of Official Languages and the Office of the Commissioner of Human Rights. This environment commissioner could act in an automous fashion, being directly responsible to Parliament and directly independent of Parliament.
Passing a law would create such an office to audit policy and project assessment which signified forward thinking in the area of the environment. Within Bill C-78 itself, regulations outlined in section 55 are to be subject to the free discretion of the Governor in Council.
With direct reference to section 55(b) and (d), I feel that it is of utmost importance to define a list of projects that are to be excluded from the legislation and define a list of projects that are mandatory under the proposed assessment law.
The lists should be appended to the bill as soon as possible and before it is passed so that the rules will not be changed in cabinet later. If left to the discretion of the Governor in Council, the regulations risk not being defined as may be necessary.
The hon. minister should be more forthcoming and up front with the people of Canada by indicating early on in this bill a third list which relates to section 55(g): Acts of Parliament.
I am pleased that the hon. minister has included eight federal regular Tory statutes, and I quote: "Some provisions may warrant being covered with Canadian Environmental Assessment Act." The word "may" and not "shall". Once again, however, these are merely suggested in the act, and are not defined as concrete regulations.
The federal areas which are to come under environmental assessment must be clearly laid out and regulated.
These lists, I am sure Mr. Speaker, will become the subject of much heated debate within numerous departments, so for the sake of Canada's environment, they must be established within Bill C-78 from the very beginning.
We are now beginning to see the initial moves on behalf of several provincial governments to set up their own environmental legislation in which to counter any federal power and authority they may perceive to be a threat to their own interests.
The Minister of the Environment from Quebec, for example, has said that his province will be forced to enact its own dormant legislation. He feels that it must move quickly, before federal legislation is in force, to enact an idle section of the Environmental Quality Act.
This federal environmental assessment proposal, which will screen industrial projects for their environmental impacts, will however force the provinces to occupy their field of jurisdiction. Quebec perceives this to be a threat to its projects that involve, for example, the export of its electricity.
With the form of this legislation, we are going to see a scramble by provinces to set up their own environmental impact assessment legislation for large projects like aluminum smelters, pulp and paper plants and hydro dams.
The design of these provincial assessment legislations could over-ride the benefit of federal legislation. The provinces see an urgency to protect their own industrial development and will not hesitate to assert their control of their interests.
Other provinces have jealously condemned the loss of jurisdiction by taking pains to ensure that their environmental assessment legislation is comparable to the federal government. This government will lose the strong position it held with the court decisions.
Therefore, within this legislation, there is an absence of a mechanism which will ensure compliance to Bill C-78.
June 26, 1990

This thorny question of federal-provincial jurisdiction has been largely sidestepped in this bill. The hon. minister promises that the jurisdiction will be spelled out once again in the regulations yet to be proclaimed. The hon. minister is offering us promises with potentially wide range negative impact.
As an example, I will refer to the D'Arcy McKeough dam and diversion which is in the riding of the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex and of which he will be well aware. This project was to save the town of Wallaceburg from spring flooding.
The politicians and bureaucrats decided to expropriate the area required without due respect for the owners. Now no one likes the idea of losing his or her property to expropriation, but if fairly compensated and to help neighbours, there are no problems.
Common sense did not prevail, as the government wanted the land for nothing. Those affected by this expropriation formed a committee referred to as SOS, Save our Sydenham. The battle was on. At the examination for discovery, after many days of hearing witnesses, the judge ruled in favour of the SOS committee. To make a long story longer, a project that originally was to cost approximately $7.3 million ended up costing the provincial and federal governments in excess of $40 million.
At that time I sat on both the SOS committee and on the St. Clair Conservation Authority. You can imagine my frustration, due to a conflict of interest, in not being involved when the dam and diversion topic was discussed and watching millions being wasted every year. In the end the dam and diversion were built. The owners were properly compensated and the town of Wallaceburg was saved from flooding in the spring. In the process of not having guidelines, the government blew over $30 million. This is only on a small project.
In discussing Bill C-78, it is also important to draw attention to the fact that Canadian foreign aid, Crown corporations and support for Canadian exports abroad, will be subject to special rules still to be determined within the legislation. Again, it is important to the substance of this bill that policies with international implications be a part of the immediate act.

To close, I would like to point out one final weakness in Bill C-78.1 question whether this bill entails the most efficient and effective method in which to utilize the additional $100 million in allotted government funding. The government has reached the point where it must really turn things around as far as its efforts toward the environment go. This environmental assessment bill could become a cornerstone for Canada if only the government would take a few larger steps further to create a more dynamic piece of legislation.

speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. Member for Prince Albert-Churchill River (Mr. Funk)-The Goods and Services Tax; the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Cowichan (Mr. Stupich)-The Fisheries; the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons)-The Fisheries.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to participate in debate on Bill C-78, the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act.
I must say I am a little bit surprised at the order because, indeed, I thought my colleague across the floor would speak first. I was looking forward to hearing what she might say.
The concern of the people of Canada for the environment was very evident last year when we came back to this House as a new government, newly elected and set up new committees. I noted that every committee was working on environmental issues involved with their particular interest. Out of that concern grew my work on parliamentary reform and global climate change. It emphasized to me that everyone in all aspects of life is getting more and more concerned, and I am delighted that this government is demonstrating its concern and interest by introducing Bill C-78.
Bill C-78 outlines a legal process, establishes ground rules and creates an efficient balanced approach for the environmental assessment process. In addition, this bill guarantees the public that they can participate in the process and be able to influence government decisionmaking. In this way, this legislation provides the most fair and open environmental assessment process in Canada and, indeed, in the world. This government is acting on the concerns of Canadians and the recommendations of the World Commission on Environment and

Government Orders
Development, the Brundtland commission. The World Commission added new impetus and focused growing public demand for reforming environmental assessment processes. In its report, "Our Common Future", the commission concluded that the environmental assessment processes would be more effective if they were mandatory and entrenched in legislation; this is what we have done.
This reform package that we have introduced will ensure that all decisions of the federal government fully integrate environmental considerations where these are relevant to ensure protection of our natural environment and for future generations of Canadians. We believe, indeed we know, that many of the environmental problems we are forced to deal with today could have been avoided if we had simply improved the way in which we have planned in the past and we will do that by planning better in the future. Before we begin a project, it is just as important to know if a project is environmentally viable as it is to know what capital and labour resources are required to make it viable in economic terms.
It is not the intent of this government to use this legislation to stop projects, but rather to ensure that environmental impacts are considered before a project proceeds. This is the only sensible and fair thing to do, to protect the rights of future generations of Canadians to an environment equal or better to the environment we inherited from our parents. This government has gone to great lengths to make sure this legislation is the most fair legislation possible.
Let me start by showing this House how the whole process we have introduced is a fair one. For example, it would not be fair to the Canadian taxpayer to conduct environmental assessments of projects we know would not damage the environment. For this reason, we have proposed an exclusion list to be compiled through public consultation. The list will include projects known not to pose any risk of harm to the environment or where environmental effects are negligible. Projects such as simple renovations, routine operations, purchasing supplies or minor construction would be exempt from this review. However, we also believe it would be unfair not
to conduct assessments on projects we know will impact on the environment, so we have proposed a mandatory study list. Projects on the mandatory study list will be large-scale projects that often generate considerable public concern, such as large oil and gas developments, uranium mines, major hydroelectric developments and large industrial plants.
Perhaps I could add here that I was astonished recently to learn that dams which we have in the past always felt were not harmful insofar as the hydroelectric generation aspects are particularly difficult to manage from the standpoint of mercury contamination of the water for a few years after they are put into operation. Another major part of dam construction that I had never considered before is that of methane generation and the impact of the methane on the warming trend. New information seems to be coming forward and putting different perspectives on things that we thought before were not harmful. To ensure that the lists are acceptable to the widest number of Canadians possible, we have proposed an equal and fair opportunity to any interested individual to play a role in the development of the exclusion and mandatory lists.
Further, it would not be fair to expect industry, environmental groups and communities to spend time and money participating in environmental assessments of projects similar to ones already assessed for environmental impacts. For this reason, we have proposed a process to assign projects of a similar nature to classes for review. We have proposed that projects could be assigned to classes if they are routine, repetitive and known not to cause significant or unmitigable effects. Such projects could include dredging, highway maintenance or rebuilding of facilities on the same site. Further, it would not be fair to ask Canadians to accommodate unnecessary delay because of environmental assessments. We recognize that many projects requiring a federal decision may also require decisions from other interests, including provincial governments, foreign states or other federal authorities with similar review processes. We believe co-operation can ensure the environmental assessment process is efficient and reduces duplication of work and cost to all parties and stakeholders.
June 26, 1990

The act offers a number of mechanisms designed to overcome such duplication and inefficiency to achieve closer co-operation and co-ordination between interested parties having responsibilities in relation to the same project.
The act enables a responsible authority to co-operate in the preparation of environmental assessments with another party or jurisdiction in the case of a screening or a mandatory study. It requires the responsible authority to exercise the appropriate quality control for any assessments so undertaken. It does not, however, allow the responsible authority to delegate any of its decisionmaking powers.
This feature will enable federal authorities to work closely with other parties and jurisdictions to minimize duplication and confusion without sacrificing environmental values. Not only is the process fair, but the opportunities for participation are fairer than ever before. The Government of Canada believes public participation is essential to achieving an appropriate integration of economic development and environmental protection.
The Canadian Environmental Assessment Act will provide a fairer opportunity for public input at all stages of the assessment process. Under the act public participation will be encouraged in a number of ways.
For instance, public participation will be enhanced through early notification. Responsible authorities will be required to inform the public through public registries and newspaper ads of major project proposals at an early stage of the assessment process. Public comments will be invited at that time. Time periods for the receipt of comments and information will be established by the agency.
Also a public registry will be established for each project, containing reports and supporting documents and information used in the assessment of the projects and the course of action following completion of the assessment. The public will have full access to the registries. The Access to Information Act will apply with respect to any restricted information.
Mediation will also enhance public participation. It will involve representatives of public groups which have
Government Orders
a direct interest in or are directly affected by a proposed project.
Mediation is fair on two counts. First, it provides a fair opportunity for interested parties, opponents, and supporters to participate in an environmental assessment. Second, it reduces the time and money required for full assessments in cases where it appears all stakeholders are willing to participate and consensus is considered to be possible.
To maintain neutrality the Minister of the Environment, rather than the proponent or the responsible authority, will appoint the mediator. The mediator will assist and advise participants, not make decisions for them.
Panel reviews will also provide equal and fair opportunities for stakeholders to participate in developing recommendations on a project for the Minister of the Environment. Review panels will conduct their deliberations independently of the government. Review panels will be required to hold public hearings to allow the public to present its views and recommendations.
To assist public participation, the reform package includes a participant funding program to ensure that stakeholders have the opportunity to participate and play a full role in panel reviews and mediation.
The purpose of the financial assistance program is to improve the fairness and effectiveness of public reviews by increasing the equality of participation. It will help achieve balance and objectivity of decision making by supporting the preparation and presentation of informed views for decision makers that might otherwise not be available.
Further, Canadians will have the opportunity to comment on each individual act regulated under the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act. This government could have included a list of acts in the actual legislation. This would have provided Canadians with only one opportunity to comment on their inclusion, but the process that we have proposed will allow Canadians to comment on each regulatory statute to be included. Indeed, I believe it gives the government greater latitude to include other acts than it would if we had to choose them all at the present time.

Government Orders
Finally this government recognizes that it is only fair to lead by example. For this reason, while debate continues on the proposed legislation and Canadians make submissions to the legislative committee with regard to this legislation, we will begin immediately to consider the environmental implications of all proposed policy.
The results of the environmental assessment of policies will be integrated into the analysis supporting the policy proposal and will be incorporated into the memoranda to cabinet.
For the first time there will be routine environmental assessments of all federal policy proposals coming before the cabinet. This is a very important element of the reform package which accompanied the introduction of Bill C-78.
In summary, we are debating a bill in which everyone in this House can take pride. I am certain that we are examining a bill which will be a cornerstone of Canadian environmental policy for years and generations to come.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member could respond to a very deep concern that there is in much of Canada about the 1984 cabinet guidelines order.
As the member knows, in Saskatchewan the Rafferty-Alameda project is proceeding even though the Government of Canada is paying Saskatchewan $1 million a month not to proceed. Supposedly it is proceeding on the basis that this is safety related work. I do not think anyone would dispute in relation to any large project where there is such a scrambled jurisdictional omelette as the Rafferty-Alameda that safety related work should be completed.
There does not seem to be a distinction between safety related work and completion construction. The same is true in Alberta with the Oldman development despite a unanimous ruling of the federal Court of Appeal that the project should not proceed until an environmental assessment has been done, both on transport matters in relation to the Navigable Waters Act and in relation to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
My question to the hon. member is this: How can Canadians trust a piece of legislation which does not either include the statutes, the exemption list or many other things the government says it will put in it, like intervener funding at some point? We have the Rafferty-
Alameda project running contrary to a Federal Court ruling and the Oldman proceeding despite a unanimous ruling of the federal court of appeal.
What should be done on those two, and should the other statutes not be included?

Mr. Speaker, obviously I cannot answer all the hon. member's questions. My involvement in environmental affairs is more recent than his own. Indeed he knows all the background to the particular questions he has asked.
It would seem to me that under this act, with the ability to review projects before they get going and before they are put in place, any of the problems he is signifying seem to be occurring with the Oldman dam and the other dam out west would be avoided.
He should be applauding the government for taking action and presenting a bill today that could avoid such problems in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is unfortunate when an hon. member rises, delivers a speech, and is not as familiar as one might be with the subject matter, or he would know that the answer he just gave the House does not really reflect reality.
The courts have been quite clear that the government has not only the power but the obligation under the existing legislation to conduct an environmental assessment in any area of federal responsibility. This obligation which I will be speaking to shortly is in fact weakened by this legislation and not strengthened.
The government asks us to take a great deal under this legislation on faith. I wonder if the hon. member would tell us how the government intends to demonstrate that faith by complying with the orders of the court in the Oldman River Dam in carrying out, as directed by the court, an environmental assessment by the Minister of Transport and by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to ensure that the project is not further proceeding as it is now, totally illegally and without the required permit from the Government of Canada under the Navigable Waters Act.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether I should be very annoyed, just a little annoyed, or quite what my reaction should be to the member's elitist. Because the member is very informed with her background in environmental processes, she feels that I as a newcomer to the field with an interest and a deep

concern for my family, for my grandchildren, should not be able to comment on a bill before the House. I believe that is narrow in perspective and totally unfair to the process. Indeed I am learning about the process as I go on. I believe that is a right and a privilege that I should have freely in this House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the very important matter of the environment and as a member who serves the area wherein the Rafferty-Alameda dam is located, one of the very disturbing factors is that we get many comments and many opinions cast before people understand the project.
If we are truly to have a good environmental approach, which we all want to see, I think that the opposition and government people will have to take some responsibility in terms of knowing what they are talking about.
I will give you an example. One of the people who has been most outspoken on this issue said that there were 2,400 acres of trees in the valley. There is one little grove of trees in the valley. There are people passing comment without even seeing the project.
It is safe to say that 90 per cent or more of the people there, whether they are Liberal, NDP, or Conservative, say that we need water in that area. This matter has been studied since 1905, and this type of approach does not help provide a good direction for environmental concerns and issues.
If we are to have sustainable environmental development, we have to take a balanced approach and we must know what we are talking about in dealing with individual projects.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see this bill before the House. We have been anxiously awaiting it for a long time. Other members who have been in the House longer than I have been here were awaiting it long before I was. It is indeed a pleasure to have it before the House and to have an opportunity to have it referred to a committee for detailed study and, I would hope, some substantial strengthening and improvement.
As I see the bill, it is in fact a step backward from what we now have in place. The courts have been very clear as to the strength of the guideline orders that are currently in place and have been since 1984.
Government Orders
They have been very clear that the guideline order places on the government and on every agent of the government, specifically on every minister, not the possibility but the responsibility to do a full environmental assessment of any project that touches on a minister's area of responsibility.
The courts have been very clear that the effect of the guideline orders is all inclusive and pervasive. It is therefore very disappointing to see before us in this long awaited legislation a bill that is intended to exclude more than to include, a bill that sets up a framework for the government to do the least possible rather than the best possible.
We have a situation where in fact how good this legislation is or how effective it is in protecting our environment depends very much on how the government chooses to use it. The guideline orders show that the government has chosen in most cases to get away with the minimum it can rather than do the most it can do. It is disappointing. At this stage, particularly with the level of public awareness of a new approach to the environment that is much broader than simply not dirtying the water and not fouling the air, the legislation does not deal with the concept of sustainable development. In fact, it specifically excludes those factors from being taken into consideration. They are important issues such as the unwarranted waste of resources, especially nonrenewable resources. The whole purpose of preserving our environment for future generations and changing the way we behave and operate is so that that objective is achieved. A good part of that is based on, not temporary damage to certain aspects of our environment, but whether we even will have enough resources left in the future on which to survive and thrive.
One other major issue that I feel is excluded from the bill and that I hope we will be able to consider in amendments to the bill when it is before committee is aboriginal rights. It is a shame that a small country such as New Zealand can, at this stage in its history, ensure the preservation and protection of aboriginal traditions and cultures in its comprehensive environmental legislation and a country such as Canada has not chosen to include that as a factor to be considered in carrying out environmental assessments. I do hope members of the House, particularly members of the government, are prepared to consider favourably amendments that will no doubt be brought forward to ensure that aboriginal

June 26, 1990
Government Orders
traditions and cultures are part of the environmental assessment that comes with any project.
A third major point that will need a great deal more attention when the committee addresses the bill in greater detail is the international factor. The bill very specifically excludes the Export Development Corporation. The Export Development Corporation is responsible for assessing those projects which Canada will fund to develop exports particularly to developing countries. It is irrelevant to include CIDA and CIDA projects abroad, which are overseas development aid projects, in the requirement for environmental assessment and yet not include the Export Development Corporation through which major goods and services are exported to developing countries.
The Environment Committee, through its hearings, has become increasingly aware of the importance of what we do internationally to the point where, if our concern is our global commons-our global atmosphere, our global water supply, our global supply of lands and natural areas-then we have to look very seriously at balancing what we choose to invest in Canada and elsewhere in the world in terms of protecting the environment.
It makes absolutely no sense for us to cut back on environment-destroying technologies in our own country while, through the Export Development Corporation and its assessment of projects, continuing to finance the export of projects to developing countries without any consideration whatsoever as to the environmental impacts of those exports that we have chosen to subsidize or to finance. It simply is a truism to say that anything that goes up into the air over China, India, or Indonesia, comes down in Ottawa, Toronto, Vancouver, or Rimous-ki.
I want to speak about the assessment of cabinet policy. I understand very well the tradition of cabinet secrecy and confidentiality and the reasons why material that goes to cabinet cannot be public. However, given the statements of the government and the concern of the public, I am shocked to find that an environmental statement or consideration is not already a required item on material going to cabinet. I believe that this is an extremely important weakness in the bill in that cabinet decides on the spending of many billions of dollars. It decides on significant expenditures on physical projects that have great potential to damage the environment. It
decides on energy policies which have significant potential either to help or harm the environment.
In my view, the public is entitled to know on which considerations those decisions have been made, what their impact on the environment will be, and whether or not they are good policies from the point of view of the environment. The legislation does absolutely nothing to give the public that assurance. One can achieve that quite easily, respecting cabinet secrecy and at the same time respecting the public's right to know, by simply guaranteeing in the legislation that, once determined by cabinet, every policy will be subject to an environmental assessment review as any other project of any other private sector individual. The results of that assessment will be made known to the public and they will have opportunity for input and comment.
I want to speak about some of the loopholes in the legislation which I certainly hope we will be able to do something about when we come to deal with this and report back to Parliament on the legislation.
First, we start with projects on federal lands. However, we exempt those lands which the federal government has previously sold or any sale of federal lands unless there is a specific project. The government should, as a public owner of land, assume that it has a public responsibility of public trusteeship and when it disposes of land, for whatever purpose it is disposing of or leasing land, it should be subject to an environmental assessment. The sale in itself constitutes a project or an activity of government that should be subject to an environmental assessment.
I am concerned about weak-kneed wording such as "shall include a consideration of" and "mitigation without definition". I am concerned that the scope of factors to be taken into consideration by any responsible authority, and that includes a minister, shall be determined by the responsible authority. In other words, if I am sitting there as a minister sometime wanting to build some major big project, I have the right under this legislation to decide on what terms and conditions the environmental impact of that project shall be considered. Obviously, that has got to be tightened up.
June 26, 1990

We have the words "serious environmental impact use" and "significant environmental impact use", without attempting in any way to define those. A minister at any time could assume that, even though he has identified environmental impacts, they are not significant or they are not serious. Obviously, we have to clean up some of that.
In comparison to the guideline orders presently in existence, I notice the legislation does not give due attention to public concern. Currently under the guideline orders, any project about which there is public concern about the environmental impact must be subject to an assessment. That completely disappears from this bill. I do have trouble accepting the words of the hon. member who said earlier that this bill is a step forward and that it leaves behind guidelines that are ineffective and insufficient and puts something stronger in place. On reading the bill, it is evident to me that is not the case. In fact, if the bill cannot be strengthened, we would do better to stick with the guideline orders and the court interpretations that we now have on those guideline orders. They are comprehensive, inclusive, and far more widespread in the kind of projects that need to be assessed.
In bringing forward this legislation, the government has, in essence, given itself a great deal of power to exempt virtually anything from an environmental assessment. That is something that is not acceptable. This is far too important, not only for the future of our country and for the assets we hope to pass on to our children, but for the future of the world. We are on the brink of destroying the ozone layer that protects life on earth from ultraviolet radiation. We are on the brink of massive climatic change if we do not act. Yet, we have wishy-washy legislation before us that is a step backward from where we are now, not a step forward.
There is a great listing on page 33 of the bill of everything the government can do to exempt projects, ministries, or agencies of the government from the requirements of this act. If the government is serious, it will put forward a list now of legislation, act, ministries, and agencies that are subject to the acts. It will make a comprehensive and all-inclusive list and it will agree that there may be additions to that list by that regulation but removals may only be made by Parliament. That is the
Government Orders
only thing that protects us and ensures public scrutiny of how the government operates under this legislation.
With all those powers, the government is essentially saying: "Trust me. Trust me to do what I say I am going to do." I think we have had good reason in the last six years not to trust the government, particularly since November, 1988.
I need only remind the public and members of the House of the many sacred trusts that have been violated and of the statements by a minister in Newfoundland that the government would not touch unemployment insurance and within months we were slammed by a retrograde UI bill. We have had statements by the Prime Minister himself, pledging his loyalty to his mother and swearing he would not touch old age security. We have had a number of bills before us that do exactly that. They touch pension plans in a detrimental way.
We are being asked to trust the government that decimated its investment in alternative energy from $500 million down to $50 million. It did this at a time when it is going to international conferences and talking about the importance of alternative energy and reducing the dependence on non-renewable fossil fuels. Yet, its actions speak louder than its words.
This is the first year the Department of the Environment itself has recovered from the massive slashing of its funds that has taken place over the years that this government has been in power.
There is the Oldman River dam where, despite a unanimous court decision, the Minister of Transport states it is okay for him to let this project go ahead without a permit required for safety reasons. If he is sincere about that, he should issue a revised permit that sets out clearly what is allowed to be done at that project and that establishes clearly that the works to be done are those related to safety and safety alone. Not having done that, he and his colleagues have shown clearly that they are ignoring the order of the courts and ignoring the environmental assessments required to be done. He has abandoned any control over that project that he is required-not able but required-to exercise under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. This is the government we are being asked to trust.
I spent the best part of yesterday and today at Green Plan consultations. I heard a great deal of scepticism in a roomful of primarily business people and business organizations, not environmental groups. I heard scepticism about the intentions of the government, because, again,

June 26, 1990
Government Orders
this is the government we are being asked to trust. It had a green strategy that was ready to be brought forward last February.
We, who are members of the environment committee, put ourselves under a great deal of pressure to try to produce recommendations for the minister at a time that would have supported provisions in the budget to implement the green strategy. That was last February. Now, here we are into summer and we are back to an amorphous, meaningless discussion document that lays out no options, gives no costs and gives no analysis of the pros and cons so that thousands of people who participated in these consultations can sit down and, rationally, in a well informed manner, give the government their advice. That is the kind of frustration I was listening to this morning and all day yesterday.
Businesses are saying what businesses have always said: "Tell us the environment in which we have to operate and we will operate in that environment." They want to know the rules, they want to know the regulations, and they want to know that these rules and regulations are not going to change from moment to moment, from month to month or from fiscal year to fiscal year. This bill does absolutely nothing to give them the security that the environment will be protected. It is not only non-governmental organizations and environmental groups that are concerned about the environment. They want to do their part in protecting it but how can they? How can they, when the government can prescribe a list of projects for which an assessment is not required, prescribe a list of classes of projects for which no assessment is required, prescribe anybody to be a federal authority or not to be a federal authority? How can the citizens of this country know what they can expect from this government if it is not prepared to put it into legislation? How can our provinces know what they can expect and what requirements they have to meet if the legislation is not clear, is not immutable and not subject to the political convenience or the whims of a government?
We have already seen how the Ministry of Industry, Science and Technology considers the environment. The environment that provides for things that are not immediately of tangible value but have some higher value, poetry, music, what have you, as if care for the environment is something we can do without. We know that this legislation has been weakened. It has been weakened by a cabinet that is weak-kneed and unprepared to do what
the Canadian public wants it to do. I challenge members of the government, as we go into committee with this, to please be prepared to make it clear, precise and strong.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Ottawa West has given us a very thorough and interesting analysis of the bill before us. She has put forward some interesting views about aboriginal rights and about the international dimension of this bill. She has reviewed the performance of this government in relation to the Oldman River dam. We know that the hon. member for Ottawa West has been quite active in this House on the question of the Rafferty-Alameda project. In view of the intervention made just a few minutes earlier by the member for Souris-Moose Mountain, I would like very much to hear the views of the member for Ottawa West as to the performance of this government in relation to the Rafferty-Alameda situation.

Mr. Speaker, I really do not have to comment on it, the courts have done that adequately and fully. The courts have said that the government failed miserably and completely to accept and to exercise the responsibility it had under the existing guideline orders and that it has failed since then to act as it should act.
The courts have made it clear that on any project under federal authority, not limited as this bill is to projects on federal land or funded by the federal government, the federal government and the federal minister under whose authority it comes, can and must act to carry out an environmental assessment to protect the interests of the public of Canada and to protect the natural heritage of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to join in this debate. Following the previous speaker, it is very good to have an opportunity to put some facts forward. It is tempting to go through the comments that the previous speaker made one at a time and answer some of the rhetoric that was put forward. This particular government does not have to take any lessons from the previous Liberal administration. Being a member in Queen's Park in Ontario for a number of years, I am aware that the province of Ontario has had an Environmental Assessment Act since, I believe, 1977 or 1978. From that period of time through to 1984 the government that was in power during federally was a Liberal government. Did that Liberal government act to bring forward environ-
June 26, 1990

mental assessment legislation? Veiy clearly the answer is no.
Just prior to the federal election in 1984 it brought in guidelines which it hastily threw together in the form of an Order in Council. These guidelines were intended to be just guidelines. They were never intended to come under the microscope of the courts. Clearly, although some of the members have stated that this act is not a step forward, I think the facts speak quite differently. I do believe that this is a major step forward. The bill has been under public consideration for some period of time has been put together as a result of that public consideration and I am very pleased to have an opportunity to speak to this bill.
It is the view of the government, and certainly my view, that the environmental assessment act is a major step forward in our nation's campaign to preserve and enhance our environment. The bill is central to the over-all goal of the government's Green Plan, to make Canada the industrial world's most environmentally friendly country by the year 2000.
Certainly this act has the power in its impact of decision-making that it is the most significant environmental assessment legislation anywhere in the world. The bill will, for the first time, entrench in legislation the federal government's obligation to integrate environmental considerations into its project planning and implementation processes.
Given the immense importance of this legislation, I wish to briefly outline the four key principles used in designing the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act.
First, the government wanted an environmental assessment process that is clear, consistent and effective. There should be no uncertainty in the environmental assessment process.
Second, the process should be efficient and fair. Each project should receive the amount of time and the kind of assessment that it requires.
Government Orders
Third, the government wanted the legislation to anticipate and to prevent problems rather than adopt the less effective and more expensive approach of react and cure.
Fourth, the legislation must encourage open decisionmaking and provide opportunities for the public to play a role in the final decision.
It is this final point, the openness and the increased public participation which I want to spend a few brief moments talking about. I believe that public participation in the environmental assessment process is central, and indeed essential, to achieving both a strong economy and a healthy environment.
I am pleased to say that the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act will provide greater opportunities for all Canadians to participate at every stage of the environmental assessment of individual projects. Further, the act strengthens the public participation in assessment of major projects. The act outlines several ways in which public participation will be improved. It stipulates that the public must be notified early in the assessment process of all major project proposals.
Canadians will be invited to comment on the project proposals at this time. Similarly, the bill stipulates that the public must be notified when the Minister of the Environment receives an assessment report.
As well, for the first time open public registries must be established for all assessed projects. These registries will be a holding tank for reports and documents used in the assessment of the project. Decisions taken on proposed projects, including any mitigating measures and follow-up programs required, must also be kept in the public registries.
I think it is important that we make this very clear. All submissions, anything relating to a project, is in this open public file. Any correspondence, any materials that relate to that project are available for the public to read and they can use that material in formulating their own ideas and their own submissions for those projects. I think this is one of the most significant advancements here and it is on all projects.
The establishment of open public registries is a significant improvement in the Canadian environmental assessment process. Registries currently exist for some projects. However, they are maintained on a voluntary ad hoc basis.

June 26, 1990
Private Members' Business
Of course there will be many opportunities for Canadians to participate directly in the assessment process through the public review of major projects. Public reviews will generally be held on major projects which pose significant risks to the environment and about which the public has serious concerns.
The act introduces mediation as a new option for public review. Mediation will involve representatives of public groups which have a direct interest in, or are directly affected by, a proposed project. Through mediation, representatives will attempt to reach consensus on the potential environmental effects and measures for mitigating these effects.
Mediation is the preferred choice whenever all stakeholders are willing to participate and a consensus is considered possible. A major advantage to mediation is that Canadians who are most involved with, and most concerned about, a proposal can communicate directly with one another.
Major projects which are not suitable for mediation will be subject to public hearings by review panels. These hearings will allow all interested Canadians to present their views and recommendations.
It is important to note that under the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, the Minister of the Environment will decide on the need for public review. Under the current Order in Council guidelines, only the minister responsible for the project had the authority to order a public review.
Now it is in the hands of the Minister of the Environment alone, not in the hands of the various ministers who are responsible for those projects in the past.
I am pleased to remind the House that this government has established a formal participant funding program to ensure that all stakeholders have the opportunity to participate in these mediations and public hearings.

At the end of 1988, Mrs. Claire Lecault of Amos, asked me to make representations to the Canadian government so that family allowances be paid at the beginning of September each year, before the return to school.
Other people in my riding came to see me several times to discuss the project, at the beginning of 1989.1 have received a petition signed by people from

Senneterre, Val-d'Or, Hull, Ottawa, Saint-Jerome, Gatineau and Obaska, asking the federal government to pay family allowances at the beginning of September each year before a new school year in Canada, to help families who have one child or more in school.

Changing the date of issue of the September family allowance cheque, for the first or the second day of the month, would require amendments in the regulations. It would also require a change in the expiry dates, and the period of time during which changes can be made in the accounts would be shorter. For instance, there would be less time to change the address on a cheque between August and September.
The addresses on the September family allowances are used by Revenue Canada for the anticipated allocation of the child tax credit. If an earlier date in September was settled on, Revenue Canada would end up with a greater number of no longer valid addresses.
The minister answered my petition: "This suggestion is not unreasonnable per se and the Department's officials will assess it carefully during the computer systems review. However, considering the significance of the required changes and the inter-relationship of these programs, the Minister of Health and Welfare cannot guarantee that this suggestion will be implemented".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise and speak in favour of the motion which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the regulations made under the Family Allowances Act to allow monthly benefits for the month of September of each year to be paid for each eligible child after the first but before the sixteenth day of September, in order to help Canadian families financially at the start of a new school year.
I congratulate the hon. member for Abitibi for putting forward this very thoughtful motion.
Many expenses are incurred by parents at the beginning of the school year in September. There are new clothes to be bought, new school supplies to be had and bus passes to be purchased. At some schools there are school uniforms to be bought and tuition fees to be paid.
For these and other reasons it is necessary that we as legislators do what we can to alleviate the financial burden with which parents are confronted at that time of the year.
I therefore fully support this motion which would have the effect of expediting receipt of family allowance benefits by parents for the month of September each year. Receipt of the cheques at the very beginning of the month would make a positive difference for families whose cash flow at that time of the year is low. Families who may have experienced the need for borrowing to meet these expenses will have additional funds available when they are most needed, and not two weeks later.
Indeed, I believe that it will make a substantial difference for those families most in need, for those families with several children who are living below the poverty line. It is precisely families such as these which will benefit most from this progressive measure. To them we, as parliamentarians, have a duty and an obligation to act.
The motion being proposed has, I submit, a high benefit/cost ratio. Thousands of low-income families will experience less financial pressure in September, rendering the expenses associated with education not a disincentive to pursuit of learning.
Today there is in Canada a great need for a comprehensive policy on family issues which will have the effect of making life easier for families which experience difficulty in making ends meet. Such a policy would consider the social as well as the financial needs of Canadian families and do what can be done to reduce and eventually eliminate the scourge of child poverty, a very real problem in Canada despite our nation's great wealth. The measure before us, taken together with other measures which consider the plight of the less privileged, will improve the social fabric of our country.

June 26, 1990

Therefore, I congratulate the hon. member for bringing this thoughtful motion before the House, and in the interest of those families most in need and of their school children's education, I urge all colleagues, particularly those on the government side which controls the majority, to allow speedy passage of this private members' motion in order to help Canadian families at the start of a new school year.
