speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to respond to the motion by the hon. member for Abitibi which suggests that the government consider amending the Family Allowances Act to allow for the payment of family allowances in September of each year between the first and sixteenth day of the month. The government appreciates and shares the hon. member's concern that Canadian parents have access to their family allowances in time to help cover the costs which come at the start of a new school year. At the present time, from January to November, the family allowance cheques are delivered by the twentieth day of each month. The only exception is December, when the family allowance cheques are delivered by the fifteenth of the month to help parents with holiday season expenses on behalf of their children.
We have had a universal program of monthly allowances for parents with children which has served generations of Canadians for over 40 years. The government recognizes that the objective of the family allowance program is to help families with the cost of raising the nation's children. Our children are our most important resource. They are our future. Thus the family allowance program benefits all our society as it is an investment in the future of Canada.
Over the years, modifications and improvements have been made to the program culminating in the new Family Allowances Act which came into effect in 1974. Today, universal family allowances are payable each month on behalf of all dependent children under the age of 18. The amount of the 1990 monthly benefit is $33.33 for each dependent child. In Alberta and Quebec, the rate is different as those provinces have chosen to vary this rate according to the number of children in the family and/or their ages. In each month of 1990 the government is distributing 3.7 million cheques to families across Canada on behalf of approximately 6.6 million children.
Private Members' Business
In light of current socio-economic changes the government believes that the system of delivering child benefits must be reviewed periodically to ensure that the needs of Canadian families and their children be met. In 1984 the government began restructuring the over-all system for child benefits so that the greatest benefits go to children in low and middle income families. Effective January 1986 the family allowances were partially deindexed to the annual increase in the Consumer Price Index in excess of 3 per cent.
As a means of offsetting the impact of partial deindexation of family allowances on low and middle income families, the government substantially enriched the child tax credit. In 1990 the child tax credit provides a maximum benefit of $575 per child. The credit is payable to low and middle income family allowance recipients on behalf of dependent children under the age of 19. Beginning with the 1988 tax year, the child tax credit is available for children in the taxation year during which they turn 18. Prior to tax reform, the last year for which a credit was claimable was the tax year in which the child reached 17.
As part of the national strategy on child care, the child tax credit was increased for lower and middle income parents who care for their children at home or who may have non-registered child care expenses. The supplement, which is payable for a child age 6 and under, is $203 for the 1989 tax year. This new supplement represents an increase of nearly 40 per cent in the over-all value of the child tax credit for these children.
In November, 1986 the federal government began making an annual prepayment of, the child tax credit for low income families in order to assist with expenses during the winter months and to discourage use of tax discounters. In November, 1990 the prepayment of $383 or the basic credit and $135 for the supplement will be sent automatically to persons whose net family income for the 1989 tax year was $16,513 or less. In the 1990 budget the government proposes to extend the prepayment to families with three or more children, provided their income does not exceed $24,769 in 1990. This measure would affect 70,000 families with a total of 236,000 children.
Taken as a whole, the changes to child benefit have reduced benefits of higher income families but substantially increased the benefits for lower income families.

Private Members' Business
Thus the government is meeting its objective of directing more assistance to low income families through the child benefit system.
In addition to these improvements to the child benefit system, the government believes that the system of delivering child benefits must be reviewed to ensure that the system is keeping pace with new technology and that the system is adequately serving the changing needs of Canadian families and their children.
Thus, in 1989, the government initiated the income security programs branch redesign project. Within the broad scope of the project, family allowance processes and procedures are being redeveloped to make use of the new technology and improve program delivery to family allowance recipients. It is expected that the redesigned family allowance system will be in operation nationally later this summer.
I am pleased to inform the hon. member for Abitibi that his motion will be examined within the context of this redesign project.
There are, however, several important factors which should be given careful consideration before any action is taken on the hon. member's motion. First, the August and October cheques would be delivered at the usual time, the twentieth day of these months. Thus the family allowance recipients would in August and September receive two family allowance cheques within a three-week period and then have to wait approximately six weeks before receiving the October family allowance cheque. It is possible that the long delay between receipt of the September and October cheques could create financial hardship in some families. Given this and other concerns, as well as administrative and operational changes that would be required, the government will proceed with a detailed analysis of the motion.
Since I have the attention of the House, I appreciate the opportunity to inform hon. members that the government is taking advantage of advanced technology, as well as responding to the wishes of a significant number of Canadians, by introducing a direct deposit service for persons receiving a federal government benefit. In 1990 persons receiving federal income security benefits such as old age security pension, Canada Pension Plan benefits, and family allowances can use the direct deposit service. Because some Canadians prefer to receive a cheque in hand, the direct deposit service is voluntary. Those who do not use the direct deposit service can have their family allowances cheque deposited with the financial institution of their choice.
There are many direct and indirect advantages to the direct deposit service. We all know how difficult it can be at times to get to our financial institution of choice to cash or deposit a cheque. With the direct deposit service such concerns are eliminated.
For example, the family allowances cheque is deposited on the due date directly to the recipient's account, thus eliminating a trip to the financial institution. Another important factor is that the funds begin to earn interest immediately. With a customer card, withdrawals can be made at the recipient's convenience.

We have heard over and over again by this government in throne speeches in 1984 and 1988, in statements by the Prime Minister, in subsequent statements by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and by almost every conceivable agent of the Government of Canada that they were very concerned with child care, only to find that those statements were not acted upon.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite surprised at the comments of the last member who just spoke.
I have been here since 1980.1 do not know how many years he has been here, but I know he was here and had
an opportunity to sit in government. It is very easy to sit here today and criticize the initiatives of the government, but at least we are taking action and doing something by providing programs for the people of this great country. From children of all ages, right through to our seniors; every aspect of livelihood is assisted in this country. This member sat here in government. I do not recall his party bringing in one initiative to help young people or seniors in the period of time that I was here from 1980 to 1984.1 am surprised to hear him criticize the government.
I want to go back and deal with the amendment that my hon. colleague has brought before us today. I compliment him on what he has already done. He has brought forward an opportunity for discussion and to take a good look at the cheques being mailed and the family services being provided to young people and parents to help them at a very needy time.
In the context of this interesting and thoughtful suggestion, I would like to discuss some of the current initiatives of the federal government in the area of improvements and delivery of social benefits to Canadians.
As hon. members are aware, family allowances are administered by the Income Security Programs Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare. The ISP Branch, which also operates the old age security program and the Canada Pension Plan, is the government's major agency for issuing benefit cheques to millions of Canadians every year.
Indeed there are few Canadians whose lives are not somehow touched by the ISP. There are, of course, the mothers who receive family allowances on behalf of their children, the workers and employers who make regular contributions to the Canada Pension Plan, the seniors who receive CPP retirement pensions, as well as old age security benefits, the lower income pensioners who receive payments under the guaranteed income supplement and spouses allowance programs, the surviving spouses who receive CPP survivor benefits, and the disabled Canadians who receive disability pensions from the CPP.
Most Canadians would be less aware of the vigorous client services, delivery and redesign initiatives currently under way at the Income Security Programs Branch. These have been specifically undertaken to streamline and fully modernize the branch's over-all operations. I do not believe we have to take a back seat to anyone or

any country in the world in the support of these programs.
The focus and commitment of the ISP redesign project is to implement the optimum level of service for clients in terms of accurate, timely and regular delivery of benefits.
The ISP redesign project is being undertaken as a joint enterprise between the Departments of Health and Welfare and Supply and Services, with additional participation from Revenue Canada Taxation, Veterans Affairs and Treasury Board. Now just look at the changes, Mr. Speaker. We will get into that some day when we talk about changes we have made to veterans programs.
Treasury Board has now allocated $7.9 million for resources to develop a comprehensive business strategy expressly for the redevelopment of the delivery processes for income security programs.
This redevelopment is now well under way. Following a rigorous evaluation, the federal government selected KPMG Peat Marwick to develop several key components in the new ISP business strategy. Among these components are a business solution which deals with how income security programs should be delivered in the future, the business change plans which deal with how to arrive at this future and at what cost, and the related business case documents and impact assessments.
In addition to the business strategy, resources have been made available to develop a comprehensive communications strategy, which will directly prepare ISP for future change, will assess and validate emerging details of the business strategy, and will provide additional support as required. The business strategy phase is expected to be completed by March, 1991, that is by the end of the current fiscal year. This will be followed by a general design phase to be carried out at the same time as preparation of the Treasury Board submission for the final detailed design, development and implementation phases.
In order to establish the general direction and philosophy for the redesign of the income security client services delivery processes, the Department of National Health and Welfare has completed a vision for income security programs. This was done in consultation and co-operation with other federal departments involved in
Private Members' Business
the policy for and delivery of income security benefits of all kinds for Canadians.
The vision will guide all subsequent developmental work and will explicitly and intimately shape the eventual business solution and business change plans. These will be concerned with such specific dimensions as human resources organization, work processes and functions, management processes, technical support systems, facilities infrastructure, and of course actual legislation, policy and regulations. Copies of this vision document are available for review by members.
I realize that some hon. members may ask: Can this wide-ranging exercise translate into real progress and tangible improvements that are directly helpful to ordinary Canadians in all walks of life?
In the vision for ISP it is emphasized that within Canada's over-all system of social programs the mandate of the ISP branch directly encompasses a strong leadership role in the evolution and delivery of the entire nation's social security policies, reflecting the spirit of democracy at its most vigorous and salutary. The income security programs branch provides benefits to Canadians in the form of direct income and thereby illustrates Canada's elemental respect for each individual's rights to exercise personal discretion in determining the most appropriate use of such income to enhance his or her life or the lives of others.
You will see in the vision a strong recognition that clients are the reason for income security programs' existence. The administration of the programs must always be seen by clients as accessible and knowledgeable, respectful and efficient, and the delivery of the benefits must meet client expectations.
In summary, I wish to assure the hon. member for Abitibi that his motion for earlier family allowance payments during September is of direct interest to the government. We will be pleased to examine his proposal in the broader context of income security programs and redesign initiatives.
As I have been discussing, the federal government fully recognizes its direct, active commitment to the people of Canada to ensure sensitive, timely and efficient delivery of their benefits, not only under family allowances but under all income security programs which play a major role in the economic well-being of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened attentively to the remarks of some of our colleagues today. I want to take a moment to congratulate the member for Abitibi for having proposed this motion. I listened to the member who just spoke and gave his remarks my undivided attention. I listened to him spell out all the acronyms of the different subdepartments of the Department of National Health and Welfare which is administering this program.
He told us about how the department administered this, how the officials of the department were doing such a great job, and what department administered old age pensions as well as family allowances and so on. After listening to him for the 10 minutes allotted to him, I still do not know whether he was in favour or against the idea. After all, most of us listened to the hon. member's words of wisdom in order to figure out whether he liked or disliked the proposition set forth by our colleague.
Let us review for a moment what it is that our colleague wants. He said in his motion:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the regulations made under the Family Allowances Act to allow monthly benefits for the month of September of each year to be paid for each eligible child after the first but before the sixteenth day of September, in order to help Canadian families financially at the start of a new school year.
To some people, perhaps the amount that is derived from family allowances would be considered small. It is not a very big cheque. But for many of the constituents whom I represent, it makes quite a difference to be able to receive that cheque. It would make quite a difference during the month of September particularly when parents are struggling, single parent families and others, who are trying to make ends meet. They are trying to send the children to school.
I am sure that to be able to get that cheque earlier in September would be of tremendous significance.

Mr. Speaker, there is also a precedent. We know that, in the month of December, family allowances cheques are sent earlier to help parents, particularly mothers
since the cheques are generally made out to them, buy what they need for the Christmas season.
The same thing applies to September with the start of the school year. I think that for some of my constituents who do not have as much money as some others, it would make a big difference if they were to receive that cheque at the beginning of the month. That would allow them to buy a new pair of shoes, a new schoolbag or anything else the children need to start the school year.
So I personnally congratulate my colleague for his initiative. I could also say a few words about this government's policy and orientation regarding family allowances and the fact that we are now faced with the deindexing of these benefits.
However, I will not get into that today, for two reasons: First, I do not want to diminish the excellent suggestion made by the hon. member opposite, and second, I think you will understand that because of this bad cold, I would rather not speak any longer than I have to. That is probably partly why the rest of my comments will be brief.
Suffice it to say, Mr. Speaker, that I support this motion, and I can inform you that as far as the people of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell are concerned, in areas of high unemployment-that applies to my riding, especially in the eastern part of the riding but also elsewhere- this initiative would make a big difference to our families.
I therefore urge hon. members to think about this proposal and support this motion. Of course, all we want is to see it passed. The motion is in no way binding on the government, and departmental officials who advise the minister on family allowance might consider the excellent ideas put forward by the hon. member and the entire House. If the minister so wishes, a study could be made by a parliamentary committee, but I don't think that will be necessary.
The procedure is quite simple. In fact, it is already being applied, as I said earlier, in December. So let's have it apply to September as well. Let us help young people, mothers and single parent families during the month of September.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, since the people in charge have already been advised of its existence, if this motion is passed today, the system could be in place by this coming September.

Mr. Speaker, my question arose from news that shellfish harvesting had been closed down near a number of pulp mills on the west coast due to the levels of toxic materials found to be in certain sea animals.
Pollution is not a new issue and yet it is relatively new in what people recognize as pollution.
I was a member of the B.C. provincial legislature when the very first legislation in that province was introduced to control pollution. At the time one of my colleagues, the New Democrat member for Mackenzie, Tony Gar-grave, asked why the legislation was not dealing with air pollution as well as water pollution.
Of course the government members laughed at him. It was a ridiculous idea that we should be interested in or concerned about air pollution. In the first place it was not important. In the second place nothing could be done about it. That was just some 25 years ago. We have come a long way since.
The chronology of events I want to talk about this afternoon starts with the closure of two pulp mills on the
Adjournment Debate
west coast, the Howe Sound pulp mill and one at Prince Rupert. The prawn and shrimp fisheries were closed because of the level of dioxins and furans found to be in those particular shellfish.
There is no word that anything was done to the pulp mills. They continued to throw millions of gallons of effluent containing goodness only knows what kind of chemicals into the ocean.
The belief even at that time was that the ocean had an inexhaustible ability to absorb almost anything that was dumped into it, whether it was industrial pollution, natural pollution, or whether it was human pollution of one kind or another. Human waste, anything like that could be just dumped into the ocean and we could forget about it. We need not worry about it any more. That was the end of it.
By 1988 the realization that we could be hurting ourselves-quite apart from what it was doing to sea life-by continuing to consume prawns and shrimp that were growing too close to pulp mills that were considered to be damaging the environment.
At that time, and perhaps even today, we do not really know how bad any of these chemicals are. Assumptions are made, and there has been some evidence that certain of them are extremely dangerous, but I do not know that the case has really been proven.
However, we are making an attempt to clean up our act. In particular we are trying to force pulp mills to clean up the water they are dumping into the Straits of Georgia. But even beyond that, we want to find out how much damage the effluent is doing and trying to find ways to control and reduce it short of totally shutting down industry.
The Environment Canada report dated July, 1988-it was not revealed publicly until Greenpeace managed to get a copy of it leaked to them-said there were 83 out of 122 pulp mills in Canada that were dumping more toxic waste into the ocean or into the waterways of Canada than was allowed by federal standards.
Again, we should have realized that we had to do something about these federal standards, finding out whether or not they were real standards and whether they should be observed, how dangerous they were, and also obliging the offending pulp mills to do something about it.

June 26, 1990
Adjournment Debate
November 24, 1989 was when I raised this matter in the House. At that time the minister said that "new and tough regulations would be enacted this year and letters would be sent to all the companies across Canada notifying them" of the new regulations.
That was 1989. To the best of my knowledge, if it has happened I have not seen it. These new tough regulations have yet to be issued. Nevertheless there have been some moves to tighten up on procedures.
On December 5, 1989 there was a leaked memo from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, from their own staff saying, among other things, that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans was closing its eyes to flagrant disobedience of regulations. It stated, "We have determined that DFO friendly corporations are parties with provincial permits, as well as the B.C. agency issuing the permit that allowed the offence will enjoy relative immunity from the Fisheries Act."
Mr. Speaker, we have not come very far and we have a long way to go. The Green Plan discussions that are currently under way, are criticized because the regulations have yet to be tabled and the Green Plan does not really have any plan for the future. On June 7, 1990, just this month, we were told, and this is after the two years work on this, that the pollution levels of 14 of B.C.'s 23 pulp mills are still greater than the provincial levels allow. As I said, we do not know how bad they are.
I consume crabs regularly on New Year's Day, it is something that is done in Nanaimo. The longshoremen get together and harvest crabs right at the pulp mill outfall and they grow best and biggest there. But are they safe to eat? No one has told us. When the shellfish harvesting was closed on the west coast, no one said how dangerous this food was. We were not told whether we could continue eating what was on the grocery shelves or what we had in our kitchens. There was no information at all, the beds were closed, no more fishing. What does one do with what you have already fished?
We have a lot to learn about these products and about the effect and danger of them. Beyond that, when we suspect there is a problem, then it is up to us to impose regulations and to make sure that the regulations are enforced. As I say, short of shutting down industry-and I know they are spending $1 billion currently to clean up their act-let's keep the pressure on to make sure that
we protect ourselves and everyone depending upon us for that kind of protection.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Environment Canada has recently completed nation-wide consultations with stakeholders on proposed dioxin and furan regulations, the thrust of which is to achieve the virtual elimination of dioxin and furan discharges from pulp and paper mills.
This is an important regulatory proposal which impacts not only on the environment but also on the food chain because marine species such as shellfish can ingest and accumulate contaminants such as dioxins and furans with subsequent public health consequences.
In fact, the Department of National Health and Welfare has, from time to time, issued advisory statements concerning dioxin and furan levels in shellfish from certain locations in Canada, notably in British Columbia. In light of the proposed regulations, it is important for people to know some facts about these substances so that they can appreciate the potential impact of proposed Environment Canada regulations.
The term dioxin, for example, does not refer to one compound but rather, to a whole family of 75 related chemical compounds. These 75 compounds are also often associated with another family of organochlorine compounds known as furans. There are an additional 135 related, yet individual, compounds in the furan family.
In test animals, dioxins and furans have produced a number of adverse health effects including cancer and birth defects. Impacts vary widely from species to species. In humans who have been accidentally exposed to these compounds, only one adverse health effect has been consistently observed; a skin condition called chlo-racne. This condition, which resembles acne, usually disappears soon after the affected person ceases to be in contact with the contaminant.
Nevertheless, the lack of evidence that dioxins and furans contribute to human health problems does not eliminate the need for further study and control of these undesirable substances. Our aim is to reduce the potential for exposure to the lowest level achievable. The proposed regulation by Environment Canada to reduce the presence of dioxins and furans to non-measurable quantities in final effluents will certainly add rigour to this aim and we will see that the new regulations are strictly enforced. In fact, the Minister of the

Environment announced last week in Edmonton that $50 million and 200 person-years would be added to his department's enforcement program.
By way of background, one might ask how scientists assessed the potential health risks associated with exposure to such compounds. An example using the food supply might be illustrative of the process.
The first step is to determine the quantity of the chemicals that humans can consume on a daily basis over a lifetime, with reasonable assurance that their health will not be threatened. This quantity, which is called the tolerable daily intake, or TDI, is based on studies carried out on laboratory animals, and takes into account data from human exposure incidents and is determined using appropriate safety factors.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be able to deal again with the question that I raised on Monday, June 18. That question had to do with the whole issue arising from the treatment of co-operatives under the GST.
It is becoming obvious to all Canadians and probably to the government as well that the GST, if nothing else, is a big can of worms and that the more the government attempts to scoop up the worms, the more they seem to be crawling away. One of the big worms that seems to have crawled away is the whole question of how the GST will be applied to the share capital of co-operative organizations in this country. Will co-ops be placed at a serious competitive disadvantage vis-a-vis other businesses, or will they have a level playing field to operate on?
Twelve million Canadians belong to approximately 60,000 co-ops across this country. The co-ops differ in size, in their nature, and in the things they do. There are consumer co-ops, housing co-ops, farm product, marketing and worker co-ops, health co-ops, and co-ops in many other sectors of the economy. They have been a very important factor in building up some of the regions
Adjournment Debate
of the country which often do not enjoy the economic benefits that other parts of the country do and often they are the last business organizations to stay in those communities.
The common denominator of co-ops is twofold: One is that it is one member, one vote and it is democratically controlled; second, the equity that runs these co-ops that makes it possible for them to operate comes from the members. In other words, co-ops are grassroots people pooling their resources in order to help do something for themselves, something even the hardest Tory heart should be able to welcome.
With respect to the GST, the co-operative system has the normal concerns that any business organization has regarding that tax, the difficulties in applying it, what would be included, and the accounting nightmares. However, it recently seemed to surface, somehow or other they communicated with the gnomes in the Department of Finance, that in fact there might be a much more serious implication for co-operative organizations. That was the Department of Finance's threat to treat the equity, the investment that people had in their co-operatives, as if it were a membership fee, as if it were the equivalent of taking out a membership in a golf club, fitness club, a cosmopolitan club, or whatever, and that these were not to be treated as equity investments, but rather as memberships.
This creates a very serious disadvantage to co-operative organizations because no other businesses have their equity investment taxed in this kind of way.
These investments take many different forms. They range from initial investments which people make in their co-operatives. In some co-operatives it is an initial $5 investment, all the way to tens of thousands of dollars in worker co-ops where a group of workers are getting together to set up a business which they themselves will run.
There are ongoing investments of several dollars a month that take place in direct charge to co-ops which gradually builds up equity. Then there is the whole business of the dividend that people enjoy from the profits of their co-operatives being reinvested in share capital in those co-ops. This can amount to huge sums of

June 26, 1990
Adjournment Debate
money. Even in my own case, it was not a huge sum of money, but $600 was enjoyed by our family in dividend from our co-op. With what the government is proposing, that $600 would now be subject to the GST. If we invested that $600 in any other business, it would not be taxed. It obviously puts a co-operative at an automatic 7 per cent disadvantage vis-a-vis its competition.
Nation-wide, the numbers are actually quite staggering. The co-op system enjoys approximately $1 billion in dividends every year in direct equity investment which would mean that there would be a $70 million loss under the GST.
The co-op sectors had a number of meetings with the Department of Finance and the government, making three arguments essentially. First of all, that dividends are taxed as if they are investment, they are not taxed as membership. There is no tax on membership actually, but dividends are taxed as an investment.
Second, they are treated as investment on the balance sheets of co-operatives under standard accounting practices. Third, the Canadian Co-operatives Associations Act very clearly defines the share capital as being similar in nature to a financial transaction like any other share purchase. These are all very clear in the law. It seems that the people who are defining these things in the government have not yet realized that.
Furthermore, there are several other problems. Obviously, they do not understand the bottom-up nature of co-operatives. Co-op Atlantic, which raised this issue with me, says it will cost them $640,000 for the bottom-up structural problems. Together with the other problems, it is going to cost them $1.6 million, 40 per cent of their equity.
The government must deal with this immediately, because if it does not it means one of two things. Either it does not understand how the co-op structure works, or it is actively discouraging the formation of co-operatives as a matter of public policy. Either one of those is unacceptable. The co-ops are asking for a level playing field and the government needs to respond quickly so that the co-ops can get on with dealing with the other problems that the GST causes them.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian co-operatives maintain their membership as a source of share capital and, as such, should not be subject to GST.
As you know, my colleague the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs) stated in the House on June 18 that the Department of Finance would discuss implementation of the GST with co-op members as soon as representations on their positions were received. The Department received the briefs only a week ago, and in fact, one of the key representations, the brief by the Atlantic Co-operative, did not arrive until yesterday.
Departmental officials-and I am sure the hon. member will be glad to hear this-have started a study of these various documents and are to continue their discussions with the co-ops in the very near future.

Mr. Speaker, I rise one more time. I would think that this means that on 40, 50, probably 60 different occasions, I have raised this very same issue. It is an issue that I have raised in Question Period on dozens of occasions, in so-called late shows such as we are involved in right now, in committees, and in this chamber alone 40 or 50 times. You know what it is, Mr. Speaker. It is fish, or more to the point, it is the devastation and the havoc that the lack of fish is creating in the inshore fishery, what we call the hook and line fishery along the southwest coast of Newfoundland, in Fortune Bay, in the Port-au-Port Peninsula, Baie St. George area and to a degree in Placentia Bay, insofar as my riding is concerned. That is where the havoc is most complete. That is where the people are suffering the most.
Why are they suffering? Because they are too lazy to get up in the morning and go fishing? Not quite. Each day during the winter fishery and during the summer fishery these people have done what they have done and their people before them, literally, for five centuries.
June 26, 1990

The night before they get their baited gear ready and early in the morning while most of us are still in the middle of a night's nap, at three o'clock in the morning, they get out of bed. Men with their wives in many cases both go fishing, or two brothers or two neighbours or three or four people. Anywhere from one to three or four people go out in those small, open boats. They go anywhere from a couple of miles to 10, 12 or 15 miles offshore. For several hours they catch fish, or that is what they used to do. Now they go out and they put down their baited gear and they do not catch any fish, because the fish are not there. You cannot catch it twice. If the French, for example, in 3PS, in the area of Fortune Bay near the St. Pierre and Miquelon Islands, have already caught the fish because they have been over-fishing, with the silent blessing of this government over the past five or six years, it cannot be caught a second time.
That is only part of the problem. In part of that coast the problem is foreign over-fishing. There are other problems on other parts of the coast. But let me bring you, Mr. Speaker, to the result of those problems. Let me tell you something about the havoc that is being created by the shortage of fish and, as I say, a problem not created by the fishermen themselves. They, with good intention and with deliberate effort and much sacrifice still go out in the morning, still bait their gear, still spend their scarce money to buy gas and bait. Indeed, they are now spending more to prepare for the fishery than they are taking in in terms of the number of fish they are catching.
I gave you previously, Mr. Speaker, an example. It is one of many dozens of examples I could quote but because this one is so graphic and in such simple terms it drives home the magnitude of the problem.
In the community of Rose Blanche on the south west coast of Newfoundland there are 147 licensed inshore hook and line fishermen. In the winter fishery, the three-month period, January, February, March, 1987, these people landed four million pounds. This year, during the same period, the same number of people landed fewer that 200 pounds of fish. Not enough to pay their expenses let alone to pay the mortgage, the loan on the boat, buy groceries and to meet other family financial commitments.
Adjournment Debate
That is not an isolated case. That story can be repeated in La Poile, Grand Bruit, Petites, Isle aux Morts, Burnt Islands, Fox Roost and Margaree. I could mention literally dozens of other communities up around the Codroy Valley, Bay St. George, down the coast from Burgeo east into Hermitage Bay, Fortune Bay, Placentia Bay. The story is the same everywhere.
For months we have been calling on this government to respond to that particular need. Lest there be confusion, the government has responded on another matter, the matter of the offshore fishery as it relates to places like Gaultois, Grand Bank in my riding, and Trepassey in the riding of the Minister for International Trade.
There is another need that has been completely ignored and nothing has been done about it. People do not have income. They have run out of UI and cannot qualify for more UI. They are hurting down there, I say to the minister. They are hurting, and you cannot buy groceries on hurt, on pain. If they could, their larders, their kitchens, their refrigerators, their cupboards would be full.
So far the minister is turning a deaf ear. If the minister responsible for UI, the minister of Employment and Immigration, had her way it would seem to me that every single community would be shut down and they would all be moved to Toronto. Well that is not what they want. They need some assistance from her and from him to tide them over until the stocks rebuild.
These people are part of and contributors to a way of life that has existed for many years, a culture all its own. Help them preserve it. Help them keep body and soul together. Help them keep their families together. Help them to cling to their communities until the stocks rebuild, if we are to believe the Minister of Fisheries, until the good times come back again. Help them bridge the gap. That is all we are asking the Minister of Fisheries. Not to wave magic wands. To do what his government has already done for the farmers of western Canada many times over, to do what his government has already done for the deep sea people, the trawler people and the people who work in those deep sea plants and come up with that kind of a program or, failing that, an extension of UI benefits, some ad hoc arrangement that will get these people over the hump. I tell you, it is quite a hump for those people and you would know how big a hump it is, Mr. Speaker, if you were there.

June 26, 1990
Adjournment Debate
They are hurting. They cannot keep body and soul together. They are calling on this government to prove it has some soul, some compassion. I ask the minister now, will he not take this case back to cabinet one more time and make the case of the people of Rose Blanche and those other communities that I could mention throughout my riding. These people, through no fault of their own, are having one very rough time as my letters, telephone calls and people in my riding tell me literally every day of the week.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like first to say that the Government of Canada shares the concern of the various communities which have recently experienced the closure of their fish processing plants. As the hon. member has indicated, why they have closed is because of the lack of fish.
We also know that many resource industries in this country have had to experience cycles and there are ups and downs in the prices of their products. We know that from September to December, 1989 a large number of workers were laid off in the mining, forestry and petroleum industries in Canada as well.
We know that the fishing industry is also subject to cycles, as well as to market fluctuations. It is an unpredictable business to be in as well because the nature of the resource base itself makes it unpredictable. The fish companies can only partially cope with this instability through diversification of fish supply.
In periods of severe downturn, fish companies have to close plants just to survive, which is very unfortunate. When a fish plant is closed, the lack of economic alternatives in many coastal communities in Atlantic
Canada makes the impact of these decisions especially difficult.
We know that sometimes plant closures allow companies to save operating costs by diverting the production to another plant that they might have somewhere else in the area, which can help them because they know that in all these plants they have fixed costs such as hydro, maintenance, insurance. Those are incurred regardless of the volume of fish that is received at that plant.
The alternative of keeping all the plants open would result in a lower standard of living for many of those people in those areas. That is not a picture of an industry which could be self-sustaining if that happened.
To wind up, Mr. Speaker, for these reasons, and what the hon. member has just brought to our attention again, as I will agree he has done many times, the government recently announced a $584 million adjustment package for the Atlantic fisheries. More specifically, it contains a Plant Workers Adjustment Program to provide further benefits to plant workers and trawlermen who have lost their jobs.
Furthermore, $146 million is being provided to foster the economic diversification within the fisheries and promote alternate employment in the areas affected by reductions in quotas and stock depletion.
As the hon. member has said, what we have often done for agriculture in Canada, we hope we can assist fisheries in the same fashion.
